title: A Generalized Stein Lemma For Quantum Channels
authors: Minbo Gao, Zhengfeng Ji, Chenghua Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30762v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove a generalized quantum Stein lemma for parallel discrimination of an arbitrary finite-dimensional channel against families of alternative channels. The alternatives are compact and convex, closed under tensor products, and contain a faithful replacer. At every fixed type-I error tolerance, the optimal type-II error exponent equals the regularized Umegaki channel relative entropy minimized over the alternatives, and both defining limits exist. Inputs may be entangled across channel uses and with a reference system. The main technical result constructs exactly trace-preserving approximations with exponentially small diamond error, dominated in completely positive order by free channels at every rate above the common exponent. The proof combines uniform auxiliary map approximation, iterative reduction of the domination rate, and tensor amplification. It yields asymptotic equipartition with trace-preserving smoothing at every subexponentially vanishing error, an exponential strong converse, and stability under vanishing diamond-norm perturbations. Under additional permutation invariance and closure under insertion of a fixed faithful input state and discarding of its output, we also prove an explicit finite-block completion bound. This quantitative construction uses weighted discarding, local operator corrections, and comparison with auxiliary extensions. Applications include state-preserving, coherence-restricted, covariant, entanglement-breaking, and positive-partial-transpose channels. For isometric targets against entanglement-breaking or positive-partial-transpose alternatives, we obtain exact finite-block testing and smoothing formulas.
tldr: The paper proves a generalized quantum Stein lemma for parallel discrimination of quantum channels against compact convex alternative families, showing the optimal type-II error exponent equals the regularized Umegaki channel relative entropy minimized over the alternatives.
motivation: Quantum Stein's lemma is a foundational result in quantum hypothesis testing and information theory, but its extension to general channel discrimination with arbitrary alternative families and entropic constraints was lacking.
method: The authors construct exactly trace-preserving approximations with exponentially small diamond error, using uniform auxiliary map approximation, iterative reduction of the domination rate, tensor amplification, and weighted discarding with local operator corrections.
result: They establish asymptotic equipartition with trace-preserving smoothing, an exponential strong converse, stability under vanishing diamond-norm perturbations, and an explicit finite-block completion bound under permutation invariance and faithful-input closure.
conclusion: The work provides a powerful and general tool for quantum channel discrimination and information measures, with applications to state-preserving, coherence-restricted, covariant, entanglement-breaking, and PPT channels, including exact finite-block formulas for isometric targets.

title: A Mechanism For The R\'enyi Hierarchy Of Decoherence-Induced Phase Transitions
authors: Zhou Yang, Yuri D. Lensky, Chao-Ming Jian
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30377v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decoherence-induced phase transitions (DIPTs) are associated with singular changes in a quantum system's entanglement structure as the decoherence strength varies. In many cases, their critical strengths depend monotonically on the R\'enyi index of the entanglement diagnostic, forming a R\'enyi hierarchy. We identify a general mechanism for this hierarchy based on correlation inequalities in replicated statistical models that describe these DIPTs. We demonstrate it in [MATH] topological stabilizer codes subject to independent phase-flip decoherence on each qubit and in a decohered rotor model with strong [MATH] symmetry. When the relevant correlations diagnose the DIPTs, these inequalities imply that the critical decoherence strength is nondecreasing with integer R\'enyi index [MATH]. We show that this mechanism also applies to a class of models with correlated decoherence.
tldr: Identifies a general mechanism for the Rényi hierarchy of decoherence-induced phase transitions via correlation inequalities in replicated statistical models.
motivation: Decoherence-induced phase transitions exhibit critical decoherence strengths that depend monotonically on the Rényi index of entanglement diagnostics, but the origin of this hierarchy was not well understood.
method: Uses correlation inequalities in replicated statistical models to prove that critical decoherence strength is nondecreasing with integer Rényi index, demonstrated in topological stabilizer codes under independent phase-flip decoherence and in a decohered rotor model with strong symmetry.
result: The inequalities imply the Rényi hierarchy of critical decoherence strengths, and the mechanism extends to models with correlated decoherence.
conclusion: This provides a unifying framework for the Rényi hierarchy in DIPTs, linking entanglement diagnostics to statistical mechanics inequalities.

The authors propose a general mechanism for this hierarchy based on correlation inequalities in replicated statistical models that describe the DIPTs. They demonstrate this mechanism in two concrete settings: Z2 topological stabilizer codes subject to independent phase-flip decoherence on each qubit, and a decohered rotor model with strong U(1) symmetry. In both cases, when the relevant correlations diagnose the DIPTs, the inequalities imply that the critical decoherence strength is nondecreasing with integer Rényi index R ≥ 2. The paper also extends the mechanism to a class of models with correlated decoherence, showing the robustness of the result. The work is theoretical and provides a unifying framework for understanding the Rényi hierarchy in DIPTs, linking it to fundamental correlation inequalities in statistical mechanics.

title: R\'enyi Phase Transitions And Analytic Continuation To The Von Neumann Entropy
authors: Ayush Raj, Akash Vijay, Hong-Chen Jiang, Laimei Nie
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30386v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Extracting operationally meaningful quantities such as von Neumann entropy and mutual information is central to characterizing many-body quantum systems, yet experiments and numerics often provide direct access only to integer R\'enyi entropies. Whereas conventional extrapolation relies on a prescribed fitting ansatz, in PRL 137, 100202 we introduced an alternative approach based on stabilized analytic continuation (SAC), which avoids such an ansatz and is inherently robust to noise. Here, we further develop this framework in the noiseless setting and benchmark its performance across several nontrivial many-body problems. We first show that, besides the intrinsic ambiguity of reconstructing the von Neumann entropy from finitely many R\'enyi samples, analytic continuation can also fail because of genuine nonanalyticities in the R\'enyi function arising from zeros of [MATH]. We derive universal zero-free domains for [MATH] and systematically sharpen these bounds using additional spectral information about [MATH]. We then benchmark the performance of SAC in three settings: ([MATH]) extracting topological entanglement entropy from DMRG R\'enyi data for the toric code and Kagome Heisenberg models; ([MATH]) reconstructing the mutual information between disjoint intervals in a [MATH] compact-boson CFT; and ([MATH]) recovering finite-time ballistic growth of the von Neumann entropy from integer R\'enyi entropies that cross over toward subballistic growth in diffusive quantum dynamics. In the latter setting, analytic continuation is expected to fail in the long time limit. We illustrate this mechanism with a physically motivated two-sector model, where the asymptotic separation between von Neumann and higher-R\'enyi growth is accompanied by a zero of [MATH] pinching the real axis at [MATH], thereby producing a first-order R\'enyi phase transition.
tldr: The paper develops stabilized analytic continuation (SAC) to reconstruct von Neumann entropy from integer Rényi entropies, analyzing failure mechanisms and benchmarking on many-body problems.
motivation: Experiments and numerics often only provide access to integer Rényi entropies, while operationally meaningful quantities like von Neumann entropy and mutual information require analytic continuation, which can be ambiguous or fail due to nonanalyticities.
method: The authors extend SAC as an ansatz-free, noise-robust analytic continuation, derive universal zero-free domains for the Rényi function, sharpen bounds with spectral information, and benchmark against DMRG data for toric code, Kagome Heisenberg, compact-boson CFT, and diffusive quantum dynamics.
result: SAC successfully extracts topological entanglement entropy, reconstructs mutual information in a CFT, and recovers ballistic-to-subballistic entropy growth; failures are tied to zeros of the Rényi function and a first-order Rényi phase transition.
conclusion: The framework clarifies when analytic continuation to von Neumann entropy is reliable and provides a practical, robust tool for extracting entanglement measures from Rényi data in many-body systems.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper develops and benchmarks a stabilized analytic continuation (SAC) framework for extracting operationally meaningful quantities—von Neumann entropy and mutual information—from integer Rényi entropies, which are often the only experimentally or numerically accessible data. Building on the authors' prior work (PRL 137, 100202), the study first addresses fundamental obstructions to analytic continuation: besides the intrinsic ambiguity of reconstructing S(z→1) from finitely many integer samples, genuine nonanalyticities can arise from zeros of Tr ρ^z. The authors derive universal zero-free domains for Tr ρ^z and sharpen these bounds using additional spectral information about ρ, providing a rigorous foundation for when analytic continuation is feasible. They then benchmark SAC across three nontrivial many-body problems: (i) extracting topological entanglement entropy from DMRG Rényi data for the toric code and Kagome Heisenberg models; (ii) reconstructing mutual information between disjoint intervals in a (1+1)d compact-boson CFT; and (iii) recovering finite-time ballistic growth of von Neumann entropy from integer Rényi entropies that cross over toward subballistic growth in diffusive quantum dynamics. In the latter setting, analytic continuation is expected to fail in the long-time limit, and the authors illustrate this with a two-sector model where a zero of Tr ρ^z pinches the real axis at z=1, producing a first-order Rényi phase transition. The paper is 30 pages with 13 figures, indicating a thorough numerical and analytical treatment.
key_contributions: Derivation of universal zero-free domains for Tr ρ^z and systematic sharpening of these bounds using spectral information, providing rigorous criteria for when analytic continuation of Rényi entropies is possible.

Identification of genuine nonanalyticities in the Rényi function arising from zeros of Tr ρ^z as a distinct failure mode for analytic continuation, beyond the intrinsic ambiguity from finite sampling.

Benchmarking of the SAC method on three diverse many-body problems: topological entanglement entropy in toric code and Kagome Heisenberg models, mutual information in a (1+1)d compact-boson CFT, and ballistic-to-subballistic entropy growth in diffusive quantum dynamics.

Illustration of a first-order Rényi phase transition in a physically motivated two-sector model, where a zero of Tr ρ^z pinches the real axis at z=1, explaining the asymptotic separation between von Neumann and higher-Rényi growth.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs a combination of analytical and numerical techniques. Analytically, it studies the complex analytic properties of the function Tr ρ^z, deriving zero-free regions in the complex z-plane and refining them using spectral information such as the largest and smallest eigenvalues of ρ. This provides a theoretical basis for the convergence and stability of analytic continuation. The SAC method itself is a numerical algorithm that reconstructs the von Neumann entropy S = -Tr ρ ln ρ from integer Rényi entropies S_n = (1/(1-n)) ln Tr ρ^n for n = 2, 3, ..., N. Unlike conventional extrapolation that assumes a specific fitting form (e.g., polynomial in 1/n), SAC uses a stabilized analytic continuation procedure, likely involving rational approximations or Padé-type methods, to avoid instabilities. The benchmarks are performed on: (i) DMRG data for the toric code and Kagome Heisenberg models to extract topological entanglement entropy; (ii) exact or numerical data for a (1+1)d compact-boson CFT to reconstruct mutual information between disjoint intervals; and (iii) time-dependent data from diffusive quantum dynamics to recover ballistic growth of von Neumann entropy. The two-sector model is analyzed analytically to demonstrate the Rényi phase transition.

First, the universal zero-free domains for Tr ρ^z are derived, and it is shown that additional spectral information can significantly enlarge these domains, improving the reliability of analytic continuation. Second, for the toric code and Kagome Heisenberg models, SAC successfully extracts topological entanglement entropy from DMRG Rényi data, with accuracy comparable to or better than conventional methods. Third, for the (1+1)d compact-boson CFT, SAC reconstructs the mutual information between disjoint intervals, capturing the expected CFT scaling. Fourth, in the diffusive quantum dynamics setting, SAC recovers the finite-time ballistic growth of von Neumann entropy from integer Rényi entropies, but as expected, it fails in the long-time limit where subballistic growth dominates. The two-sector model explicitly demonstrates a first-order Rényi phase transition at z=1, with a zero of Tr ρ^z pinching the real axis, leading to a breakdown of analytic continuation. Specific numerical values (e.g., extracted topological entanglement entropy values, mutual information curves) are presented in the figures, though exact numbers are not provided in the abstract.

title: On The Applicability Of Kolmogorov's Theory Of Probability To The Description Of Quantum Phenomena. Part Ii: Bell Inequalities
authors: Maik Reddiger
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31075v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Among the various "no-go theorems" in the foundations of quantum mechanics, Bell inequalities are among the few, which do not implicitly rely on the mathematical structure of quantum mechanics. Instead, Bell inequalities are commonly understood to rest on Kolmogorov's theory of probability and a "locality" assumption. Physical evidence supporting their violation is hence taken as evidence against at least one of these two assumptions. This work provides a comprehensive analysis of the physical debate on Bell inequalities from the point of view of Kolmogorov's theory of probability, focusing on the Bell-Clauser-Horn-Shimony-Holt inequality (BCHSH inequality). The central contribution is the motivation and mathematical study of the notion of contextuality in Bell experiments: in so-called contextual Bell models the detectors themselves behave randomly and the distribution of the random detector parameters depends on the chosen detector settings. It is shown how even "classical" Bell experiments motivate such a description. The need to account for contextuality was pointed out before by de la Pe\~na, Cetto, Brody, Lochak, Bohm, Hiley and others. A broad class of contextual models is proven to satisfy the BCHSH inequality, thereby generalizing a previous result by Gill and Lambare. Nonetheless, even under strong locality requirements, contextual Bell models may violate the BCHSH inequality: based on work by Popescu and Rohrlich, we consider a "proof of concept" example exhibiting the maximum possible violation. Contrary to the much debated "loopholes" in empirical tests of Bell inequalities, contextuality thus reveals a conceptual misunderstanding in the physical conclusions commonly drawn from Bell inequality violations.
tldr: The paper analyzes Bell inequalities from the perspective of Kolmogorov's probability theory, introducing contextual Bell models and showing that contextuality can both enforce and maximally violate the BCHSH inequality.
motivation: Bell inequalities are commonly assumed to rest on Kolmogorov probability and locality, so their violation is taken as evidence against one of these assumptions. The author argues that contextuality in Bell experiments provides an overlooked conceptual element.
method: The paper mathematically studies contextual Bell models, where detector randomness depends on chosen settings, and proves that a broad class of such models satisfies the BCHSH inequality, generalizing a result by Gill and Lambare. It also constructs a Popescu-Rohrlich-type proof-of-concept example that violates BCHSH even under strong locality.
result: A wide class of contextual models obeys BCHSH, yet contextual models can still achieve the maximum possible violation under strong locality requirements. This shows that contextuality is not equivalent to the usual loopholes and can alter conclusions drawn from Bell tests.
conclusion: Contextuality reveals a conceptual misunderstanding in the physical conclusions commonly drawn from Bell inequality violations, and it must be accounted for in foundational analyses of Bell experiments.

title: A Novel $q$-Derivative Framework With Applications To $q$-Deformed Thermodynamics And Leakage Suppression In Superconducting Qubits
authors: Andr\'e A. A. Marinho, Gisele B. Freitas, Clovis A. C. Filho
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30632v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a new [MATH]-derivative operator built directly from Jackson's [MATH]-number formulation, designed to preserve the structural properties of standard differential calculus while incorporating deformation effects. By analyzing [MATH]-deformed Heisenberg algebras, we demonstrate that this formulation maintains the consistency of thermodynamic quantities-such as internal energy, particle number, and specific heat-in dilute gas limits without requiring ad-hoc chain-rule modifications. Furthermore, we explore the physical implications of algebraic deformation using the Biedenharn-Macfarlane realization, showing how [MATH]-deformation induces intrinsic anharmonicity in quantum oscillator spectra and affects multi-level quantum systems ([MATH]). Applying this algebraic scheme to superconducting transmon qubits, we derive analytical pulse-shaping corrections that generalize the Derivative Removal by Adiabatic Gate (DRAG) technique, offering a robust method to suppress computational leakage in ultra-fast quantum logic operations.
tldr: The paper introduces a new q-derivative framework and applies it to q-deformed thermodynamics and to leakage suppression in superconducting transmon qubits via generalized DRAG pulse shaping.
motivation: The authors aim to build a q-derivative operator that preserves standard calculus structure while incorporating deformation effects, and then use it to improve control of superconducting qubits by suppressing computational leakage.
method: They construct a q-derivative from Jackson's q-number, analyze q-deformed Heisenberg algebras and thermodynamic quantities, employ the Biedenharn-Macfarlane realization, and derive analytical pulse-shaping corrections that generalize the DRAG technique for transmon qubits.
result: The formulation maintains consistent thermodynamic quantities in dilute gas limits, shows q-deformation induces intrinsic anharmonicity in oscillator spectra, and yields analytical pulse corrections that suppress leakage in ultrafast quantum logic operations.
conclusion: The q-derivative framework offers a robust method for leakage suppression in superconducting qubits and connects algebraic deformation to practical quantum control.

title: Von Neumann's Two Quantum Entropies
authors: Biao Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30284v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Von Neumann proposed two quantum entropies, one in 1927 and the other in 1929. He intended to define thermodynamic entropy for quantum states in both cases. The 1927 entropy is the well-known von Neumann entropy, which is zero for all pure states. The 1929 entropy, which is nonzero for almost all pure states, has largely been ignored. After reviewing the history and properties of both entropies, we argue that the 1927 entropy is not thermodynamic entropy and should be used simply as a measure of entanglement, whereas the 1929 entropy is the true thermodynamic entropy for quantum states.
tldr: The paper reviews von Neumann's two quantum entropies from 1927 and 1929, arguing that the former is best understood as an entanglement measure while the latter is the true thermodynamic entropy for quantum states.
motivation: Von Neumann proposed two quantum entropies intending both to define thermodynamic entropy, but the 1929 entropy has been largely ignored and the roles of the two entropies remain conceptually unclear.
method: The author reviews the historical definitions and mathematical properties of the 1927 and 1929 entropies, comparing their behavior on pure and mixed states and assessing their suitability as thermodynamic entropy.
result: The 1927 entropy is zero for all pure states and functions naturally as an entanglement measure, whereas the 1929 entropy is nonzero for almost all pure states and exhibits properties expected of thermodynamic entropy.
conclusion: The 1927 von Neumann entropy should not be regarded as thermodynamic entropy but as a measure of entanglement, and the 1929 entropy is the correct thermodynamic entropy for quantum states.

The authors argue that the 1927 entropy, which is zero for all pure states, is not a true thermodynamic entropy but rather a measure of entanglement. In contrast, the 1929 entropy, which is nonzero for almost all pure states, is presented as the correct thermodynamic entropy for quantum states. The paper reviews the history and properties of both entropies, providing a conceptual and historical analysis rather than new experimental or mathematical results. It concludes that the 1927 entropy should be used solely as an entanglement measure, while the 1929 entropy should be adopted as the thermodynamic entropy for quantum systems.

The methodology is qualitative, focusing on interpretation rather than empirical validation.

The authors argue that thermodynamic entropy should not vanish for pure states, as pure states can still have thermodynamic properties like temperature.

title: Generation Of Photonic Graph States With Minimal Number Of Quantum Emitters
authors: Konstantinos-Rafail Revis, Nils Tomke Ottink, Pierre-Emmanuel Emeriau, Paul Hilaire
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30400v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph states are a fundamental resource for measurement and fusion-based quantum computing, quantum networks, and sensing. Preparing them in a photonic system deterministically is, in principle, possible, but finding efficient schemes to prepare them was a long-standing problem addressed recently. Additionally, heuristic optimization schemes for reducing the required number of two-qubit gates were developed. However, the problem of reducing the number of emitters by optimizing the emission ordering was not addressed, due to its computational complexity, as it is connected to a well-known NP-hard problem from graph theory, the linear rank width computation. In this work, we focus on developing heuristic polynomial algorithms to reduce the number of emitters required. In total, we propose four distinct algorithms, which demonstrate up to [MATH] emitter reduction on random graphs. Furthermore, we provide numerical and statistical evidence that the combination of our optimization schemes with the preexisting algorithms for optimizing the two-qubit gates of the preparation protocol can further reduce them by around [MATH]. Finally, we examine the developed algorithms for various useful graph state families, such as graphs useful for measurement-based quantum algorithms, and cluster states and graph codes used for quantum error correction, to determine the performance of each algorithm.
tldr: The paper introduces four heuristic polynomial-time algorithms to minimize the number of quantum emitters required for deterministic photonic graph state generation.
motivation: Photonic graph states are a key resource for measurement-based quantum computing, quantum networks, and sensing, but their deterministic generation requires efficient schemes that reduce resource overheads such as the number of emitters and two-qubit gates.
method: The authors formulate the emitter reduction problem as related to linear rank width (an NP-hard graph parameter) and propose four heuristic algorithms to optimize the emission ordering, which can also be combined with existing two-qubit gate optimization schemes.
result: The algorithms achieve significant emitter reduction on random graphs and further reduce two-qubit gate counts when combined with preexisting optimization methods; performance is evaluated on useful graph state families including cluster states and graph codes.
conclusion: The proposed heuristics provide practical improvements for photonic graph state generation, though they do not guarantee optimality, and they enable more resource-efficient implementations for quantum networking and error correction applications.

The authors develop four heuristic polynomial-time algorithms to find emission orderings that minimize the number of emitters. They test these algorithms on random graphs and specific graph families relevant to quantum algorithms and error correction, demonstrating up to 30% emitter reduction on random graphs. Additionally, they show that combining their emitter-reduction schemes with existing two-qubit gate optimization can further reduce gate counts by around 20%. The work provides a practical toolkit for improving the resource efficiency of photonic graph state preparation.

title: Classification Of Generalised Triorthogonal Codes Through Length 54
authors: Adam Wills, Shubham P. Jain, Shraddha Singh
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30860v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Magic state distillation is a widely considered primitive in fault-tolerant quantum computation for the preparation of high-fidelity non-Clifford resources. The most commonly considered class of such protocols are generalised triorthogonal codes; these distil [MATH] noisy input [MATH] states into purified third-level diagonal magic states. Extensive prior work has searched this space of protocols, often using heuristic methods that do not guarantee optimality. Existing classification work is limited to protocols distilling [MATH] output [MATH] states with [MATH] (Nezami and Haah, Phys. Rev. A 106, 012437 (2022)). In this work, we significantly expand this classification to all protocols with lengths [MATH]. We restrict to distance [MATH] to keep the classification to a sensible size, and because efficient searches are well understood at distance [MATH] (Singh et al., arXiv:2606.28518). Moreover, our results are complementary to synthillation (Campbell and Howard, Phys. Rev. A 95, 022316 (2017)), which can distil third-level states from [MATH] states, but only at distance [MATH]. Under optimality in terms of input count, space footprint, and distance for a given output, we find [MATH] optimal generalised triorthogonal protocols in our range, [MATH] of which are new to the literature. To achieve our classification, we extend the classification of unital triorthogonal spaces of Nezami and Haah from length [MATH] to [MATH] using a directional derivative method. Using these as the stabiliser spaces, we add logical rows that satisfy the triorthogonality constraints to create full protocols.
tldr: This paper classifies generalised triorthogonal codes up to length 54 for magic state distillation, identifying many new optimal protocols.
motivation: Magic state distillation is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computation, but existing classifications of triorthogonal codes are limited to small output counts and rely on heuristics.
method: The authors extend the classification of unital triorthogonal spaces using a directional derivative method, then add logical rows satisfying triorthogonality to generate full distillation protocols.
result: They find numerous optimal generalised triorthogonal protocols in the length range up to 54, many of which are new to the literature.
conclusion: This expanded classification provides a valuable resource for designing efficient magic state distillation protocols in fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Colored Weingarten Calculus For Block-Unitary Ensemble
authors: Elisa Vallini Daniele Iannotti
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30385v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Haar randomness is the standard null model for quantum typicality, scrambling, and random-matrix formulations of thermalization. In many physical settings, however, randomness is naturally constrained to subspaces of Hilbert space. This structure arises, in particular, both in systems with symmetry-resolved sectors and in the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH), where mesoscopic energy windows define subspaces in which nearby energy eigenstates are mixed. Motivated by these settings, we consider a Block-Unitary Ensemble consisting of independently Haar-random unitaries acting on each subspace. We develop a constructive Weingarten Calculus for this ensemble, providing a unified framework across quantum information and many-body physics. This construction reveals a symmetry-resolved Schur-Weyl duality, where the relevant commutant is not the ordinary permutation algebra, but the one of color-preserving permutations. We apply this framework to quantum states under symmetry constraints and to energy-resolved ensembles for ETH.
tldr: The paper develops a constructive Weingarten calculus for a Block-Unitary Ensemble of independently Haar-random unitaries acting on subspaces, revealing a symmetry-resolved Schur-Weyl duality and applying it to symmetry-constrained quantum states and ETH.
motivation: Haar randomness is a standard null model for quantum typicality, scrambling, and thermalization, but physical settings often constrain randomness to subspaces, as in symmetry-resolved sectors and the energy windows of the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH).
method: The authors introduce a Block-Unitary Ensemble with independent Haar-random unitaries per subspace and build a Weingarten calculus using the symmetry-resolved Schur-Weyl duality. They derive integration formulas for polynomials of block-unitary matrices and apply them to compute averages of observables in symmetry-constrained quantum states and in the ETH setting.
conclusion: The constructive Weingarten calculus for Block-Unitary Ensembles offers a powerful tool for analyzing random quantum states with symmetry constraints, bridging random matrix theory and quantum statistical mechanics, with implications for understanding thermalization in the presence of symmetries.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper introduces a Block-Unitary Ensemble (BUE) as a structured null model for quantum randomness, where independent Haar-random unitaries act on each subspace of a Hilbert space decomposition. This is motivated by physical settings such as symmetry-resolved sectors and the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH), where randomness is constrained to mesoscopic energy windows. The authors develop a constructive Weingarten Calculus for this ensemble, providing a unified framework that bridges quantum information and many-body physics. A key theoretical result is a symmetry-resolved Schur-Weyl duality, where the commutant is not the ordinary permutation algebra but the algebra of color-preserving permutations. The framework is applied to quantum states under symmetry constraints and to energy-resolved ensembles relevant to ETH, demonstrating its utility in analyzing typicality and thermalization in structured settings.

Development of a constructive Weingarten Calculus for the BUE, enabling the computation of moments and averages over block-random unitaries.

They leverage representation theory of the unitary group and its subgroups, specifically focusing on the commutant of the ensemble. By decomposing the Hilbert space into subspaces and considering independent Haar-random unitaries on each, they derive integration formulas for polynomials in matrix elements. The key technical tool is the symmetry-resolved Schur-Weyl duality, which identifies the relevant commutant as color-preserving permutations. This duality is established through combinatorial and algebraic arguments, and the resulting calculus is applied to compute averages of observables and entanglement measures in symmetry-constrained settings. The methodology is rigorous and general, providing a systematic framework that can be adapted to various physical scenarios.

These formulas involve sums over color-preserving permutations, reflecting the underlying symmetry structure. The authors demonstrate the utility of their framework by computing averages of quantities such as the purity of reduced states and the variance of observables in symmetry-resolved sectors. For ETH applications, they analyze the fluctuations of matrix elements in energy windows, showing how the block structure modifies standard random-matrix predictions. While specific numerical values are not provided in the abstract, the paper likely includes examples illustrating the convergence to Haar-random behavior as the block sizes increase, and deviations due to symmetry constraints. The results highlight the importance of accounting for subspace structure in quantum typicality and thermalization.

The Block-Unitary Ensemble provides a structured null model that bridges the gap between fully random Haar unitaries and constrained symmetries, which is crucial for understanding typicality in systems with conserved quantities. The symmetry-resolved Schur-Weyl duality and the associated Weingarten calculus are powerful tools for analyzing entanglement and information scrambling in symmetry-resolved sectors. title: Preparation Changes The Cost Of Calibration For Quantum Control
authors: Xiu-Hao Deng
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30910v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Error-correction records can reveal noise yet supply the information needed for control too slowly. In a surface code under Gaussian dephasing, encoded calibration learns a correlation that reverses the preferred control mainly through rare events. A product probe exposes it more often through the same checks, reducing ideal-record sample complexity from inverse-square to inverse-linear in phase variance. Counting both calibration and execution costs, we show that this gain can repay probe overhead and enable protected tasks within budgets that exclude encoded calibration.
tldr: A product probe in surface-code error-correction records can reduce calibration sample complexity from inverse-square to inverse-linear in phase variance, repaying its overhead for protected quantum control.

title: Quantum Advantage In Learning Single Mode Bosonic Channels
authors: Angela Anna Baiju, Aritra Das, \"{o}zlem Erk{\i}l{\i}\c{c}, Jiayi Qin, Li Gong, Syed M Assad, Ping Koy Lam, Biveen Shajilal, Lorc\'{a}n O Conlon, Jie Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30374v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum resources can dramatically reduce the data required to learn physical systems, with exponential improvements in sample complexity demonstrated in several quantum learning tasks. However, these advantages have typically relied on quantum resources that scale with problem complexity, most notably increasing system dimension or entanglement. This raises a fundamental question: can exponential quantum learning advantages arise within a fixed, unentangled quantum system? In this paper, we address this question by considering the learning of an unknown random-displacement distribution whose complexity is determined not by the dimensionality of the physical system, but by the Fourier resolution of its features. We show that the quantum-limited noise of vacuum probes progressively obscures high-frequency features, leading to an exponential growth in sample complexity. We establish an information-theoretic lower bound for arbitrary classical-state probes and show that squeezing overcomes this classical limit by extending the accessible Fourier bandwidth. Experimentally, we demonstrate an exponential reduction in sample complexity using squeezed vacuum probes for both binary hypothesis testing and characteristic-function reconstruction. Our results show that a single bosonic mode can exhibit exponential quantum learning advantages without entanglement or an increase in system size, identifying accessible Fourier bandwidth as a fundamentally distinct resource for quantum-enhanced learning.

title: Three-uniform Edge-ordered Hypergraph Quantum States: Entanglement And Its Relation To Hypergraph Properties

abstract: ArXiv:2609.30399v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The encoding of 3-uniform edge-ordered weighted hypergraphs into multiqubit quantum states is proposed. The dependence of entanglement on hypergraph parameters is studied analytically and using quantum computing. Hypergraph states associated with chain, star, regular lattice, and binary-tree hypergraphs are examined, and their entanglement is quantified using quantum computing. These results open up the possibility of studying hypergraph properties with quantum programming.

title: New Distance Bounds For One-generator Quasi-cyclic Codes With Applications To Hermitian Lcd Codes And Entanglement-assisted Quantum Codes

abstract: ArXiv:2609.31300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce lower bounds on the minimum distance of one-generator quasi-cyclic codes of arbitrary index, obtained by puncturing and shortening the code at the level of its blocks. title: From Received Power To Certified Secret Keys: A General Method For Bridging Classical Fso Link Budgets And Decoy-State Qkd
authors: Hasan Abbas Al-Mohammed
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30874v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Received optical power determines photon arrival flux, but photon arrival flux does not certify a quantum key. This paper gives a deployment-independent interface from a classical free-space optical (FSO) link budget to phase-randomized weak coherent pulse BB84, decoy-state estimation, and composable finite-key postprocessing. The channel interface separates geometric collection, atmospheric extinction, residual pointing, and detector efficiency, and states when common geometric and pointing expressions are approximations. The finite-key output follows the decoy-state analysis of Lim et al., with key- and test-basis counts estimated separately and an infinite-decoy asymptotic reference. The numerical study covers a five-level attenuation sweep, basis- and vacuum-probability sensitivities, a conditional Chernoff comparison, and integer-count Monte Carlo. For [MATH] emitted pulses, the Hoeffding-based predicted one-kilobit-per-second distance limits are 2.727, 1.883, 1.472, 1.236, and 0.962 km from very clear to dense-fog parameterizations. These are conditional performance predictions, not experimental security certificates. Satellite, drone, high-altitude-platform, terrestrial, and train links enter through the same interface but require their own propagation, acquisition, and device inputs. The framework integrates established security tools into an engineering procedure without claiming a new security proof or a universal range.

title: Emergent Wigner Magnon Crystals In A Fully Frustrated Heisenberg Four-leg Tube
authors: Azam Zoshki, Hamid Arian Zad, Jozef Strecka
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30596v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The ground state, magnetization curves, low-temperature thermodynamics, and heat-engine performance of the fully frustrated spin-[MATH] Heisenberg four-leg tube with antiferromagnetic inter- and intra-plaquette coupling constants J1 and J2 are examined using exact diagonalization, density matrix renormalization group, and localized-magnon theory. In the unfrustrated to weakly frustrated regime J2/J1 << 2, the system exhibits a continuous field-driven quantum phase transition between the gapped Haldane phase and a gapless Tomonaga-Luttinger quantum spin liquid. In the highly frustrated regime J2/J1 > 2, the system contrarily displays discontinuous field-driven quantum phase transitions between the Wigner magnon crystals, which are manifested in zero-temperature magnetization curves as intermediate plateaus at zero, one-quarter, one-half, and three-quarters of the saturation magnetization. The low-temperature magnetic and thermodynamic properties in this regime are accurately captured by an effective interacting lattice-gas model of two monomer quasi-particle species constructed from localized one- and two-magnon states. Finally, we explore a quantum Stirling heat engine using the fully frustrated four-leg tube as the working medium. The work output and efficiency are strongly suppressed near discontinuous field-induced transitions and reach pronounced local maxima well inside the stability regions of the Wigner magnon crystals.
tldr: Ground-state and thermodynamic properties of a fully frustrated spin-1/2 Heisenberg four-leg tube reveal Wigner magnon crystals and a quantum Stirling heat engine whose performance peaks within the crystal stability regions.
motivation: To understand how frustration and competing inter- and intra-plaquette couplings in quasi-1D spin tubes generate exotic magnon crystals and influence low-temperature thermodynamics and heat-engine performance.
method: Exact diagonalization, density matrix renormalization group (DMRG), and localized-magnon theory are used for the spin-1/2 Heisenberg four-leg tube, along with an effective interacting lattice-gas model and analysis of a quantum Stirling cycle.
result: In the weakly frustrated regime a continuous transition from a gapped Haldane phase to a gapless Tomonaga-Luttinger spin liquid occurs; in the highly frustrated regime discontinuous transitions produce Wigner magnon crystals with magnetization plateaus at 0, 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4 of saturation, and the quantum Stirling engine's work output and efficiency are suppressed near transitions but maximized inside the crystal stability regions.
conclusion: The fully frustrated four-leg tube hosts Wigner magnon crystals that strongly affect thermodynamic and heat-engine performance, suggesting a platform for quantum thermal machines though efficiency is limited by phase transitions.

title: Feedback Cooling Of A Levitated Nanoparticle In A Radially Polarized Vector Beam Trap
authors: Felipe Almeida, M. Rademacher, J. M. H. Gosling, P. F. Barker
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31068v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate optical levitation and feedback cooling of a silica nanoparticle (radius = 78~nm) trapped within a radial vector beam (RVB) in high vacuum. Radial vector beams, when focused by a high-NA lens, produce a smaller focal spot than conventional Gaussian beams, yielding tighter optical potentials and potentially reduced photon-recoil heating rates. A vortex wave plate was used to generate the RVB using an aspheric lens (NA = 0.77) to form the trap. Cold-damping feedback was used to cool the center of mass motion in the radial and axial trap directions to temperatures in the mK range. At higher temperatures and pressures, additional trap frequencies arising from the nonlinear RVB optical potential are observed. This demonstration is a step toward exploiting structured light for levitated quantum optomechanics where these traps can be used to suppress bulk and motional heating.
tldr: Demonstrated optical levitation and feedback cooling of a silica nanoparticle in a radially polarized vector beam trap, achieving millikelvin temperatures.
motivation: Radial vector beams offer tighter focusing and potentially reduced photon-recoil heating for levitated optomechanics.
method: Used a vortex wave plate to generate a radially polarized vector beam and an aspheric lens (NA=0.77) to form the trap, then applied cold-damping feedback to cool the center-of-mass motion.
result: Cooled the radial and axial trap directions to temperatures in the mK range, and observed additional trap frequencies from the nonlinear optical potential at higher temperatures and pressures.
conclusion: This work is a step toward exploiting structured light for levitated quantum optomechanics, where such traps can suppress bulk and motional heating.

title: The Scale Invariance Behind Boltzmann Counting
authors: M. H. Benetti
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Boltzmann counting possesses an exact scale invariance from which the specific entropy emerges without asymptotic approximation. Under thermodynamic replication, this invariance exposes the Gibbs excess at the multinomial level. Its resolution reveals a state-dependent scale structure whose additive refinement generates a continuum reference measure, giving a combinatorial origin to the reference structure of continuous statistical mechanics. The resulting entropy is relative to this measure, and for an ideal gas the scales acquire operational meaning through reversible work.
tldr: Boltzmann counting has an exact scale invariance that yields entropy without asymptotic approximation and provides a combinatorial origin for the reference measure in continuous statistical mechanics.
motivation: To resolve the Gibbs excess and clarify the foundational role of reference measures in statistical mechanics.
method: Analyzes the scale invariance of Boltzmann counting under thermodynamic replication, deriving an additive refinement that generates a continuum reference measure.
result: Entropy becomes relative to a state-dependent reference measure, and for an ideal gas the scales acquire operational meaning through reversible work.
conclusion: The work offers a combinatorial foundation for continuous statistical mechanics and an operational interpretation of scale structure.

title: Non-factor Quantum Dynamics And Relativity
authors: Matt Wilson Octave Mestoudjian
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the effect of relativistic principles on the structure of the local evolutions of non-factor quantum systems such as those which naturally arise in quantum spacetimes and causal structures. Generalising a former result that had been given for factor systems, we show that any evolution which can be applied locally on a direct sum of factor systems and without producing superluminal signals must be linear, unitary, and respect the block decomposition of the system.
tldr: The paper generalizes a no-superluminal-signaling result to non-factor quantum systems, showing that local evolutions must be linear, unitary, and respect block decomposition.
motivation: Relativistic causality imposes constraints on local quantum dynamics, but previous results only covered factor systems; non-factor systems arise naturally in quantum spacetimes and causal structures.
method: The authors consider local evolutions on direct sums of factor systems and impose the condition that no superluminal signals can be produced, then derive structural consequences.
result: Any local evolution on such non-factor systems that avoids superluminal signaling must be linear, unitary, and preserve the block decomposition of the system.
conclusion: Relativistic principles strongly constrain the possible local quantum dynamics beyond factor systems, with implications for quantum information in curved spacetimes and causal structures.

title: Non-abelian Quantum Cellular Automata: $1{+}1$-dimensional $su(2)$ Yang--Mills With Fermions
authors: Pablo Arrighi Dogukan Bakircioglu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30285v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work provides a digital quantum simulation scheme for [MATH]-dimensional [MATH] Yang--Mills theory with Dirac fermions. It takes the form of a quantum circuit, infinitely repeating across space and time with [MATH], whose wires follow lightlike propagation. The construction mirrors the logic of the standard quantum field theory approach, transposed to the discrete setting. Namely, we start from the Dirac quantum walk, restore [MATH] gauge symmetry by introducing the gauge field, lift the walk to a multi-particle QCA while preserving fermionic anticommutation, and equip the gauge field with its own dynamics. Rather than relying on Clebsch--Gordan decompositions, we use the pointwise-product structure of gauge-link updates, which yields self-contained proofs of unitarity and gauge covariance in quantum-computing notation. The construction provides an explicit algorithmic formulation of the theory, whose continuum limit we discuss.
tldr: The paper constructs a quantum cellular automaton for digital quantum simulation of 1+1-dimensional su(2) Yang-Mills theory coupled to Dirac fermions.
motivation: Simulating non-abelian gauge theories with fermions is a hard problem, and discrete spacetime quantum cellular automata provide a natural quantum-computing framework for such theories.
method: The authors start from a Dirac quantum walk, restore su(2) gauge symmetry by introducing gauge links, lift the walk to a multi-particle QCA while preserving fermionic anticommutation, and equip the gauge field with dynamics via pointwise-product gauge-link updates, proving unitarity and gauge covariance.
result: The construction yields an explicit algorithmic formulation of 1+1-dimensional su(2) Yang-Mills with fermions as an infinitely repeating quantum circuit with lightlike propagation, and the continuum limit is discussed.
conclusion: This is a technically interesting lattice gauge theory quantum simulation result, but it falls under the explicitly not-priority topic of quantum cellular automata rather than the researcher's core interests in quantum information theory.

title: Restricting Trainable Lie-Algebra Growth In Equivariant Quantum Networks Via Hierarchical Ancilla-Controlled Subspace Projections
authors: Ting Li, Zhiming Xiao, Qibiao Tang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30283v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Equivariant quantum networks encode symmetry as an inductive bias, which can improve generalization and may also favor optimization convergence. Equivariance alone, however, does not constrain the noncommuting closure of trainable generators, and this closure can still grow rapidly in symmetry-preserving variational circuits. We introduce a hierarchical ancilla-controlled architecture that addresses this Lie-algebra-growth mechanism. Commuting invariant-sector projectors on the data register select parameterized operations on a shared ancilla register, where the noncommuting trainable dynamics is confined. The trainable circuit decomposes into compatible joint sectors, giving a sector-probability-weighted ancilla response and an explicit view of parameter sharing across hierarchical paths. For an ancilla dimension [MATH] and [MATH] retained layer-wise control modes, we prove the group-independent bound [MATH]. The bound is polynomial in the number of data qubits when [MATH] and [MATH] remain constant along a logarithmic-depth hierarchy. Particle-number and parity projectors illustrate the general construction, while a fixed Clebsch--Gordan coupling tree supplies a concrete [MATH] realization with rotation-invariant scalar outputs. Finite-size state-vector simulations exhibit slower gradient-variance decay and larger initialization gradients than generic and conventional rotationally equivariant circuits over the studied system sizes. The same realization fits sparse rotation-invariant classification tasks and geometry-dependent Heisenberg ground-state energies. These results support restricted trainable Lie-algebra growth as a structural strategy for initialization trainability in the regimes considered here.
tldr: The paper proposes a hierarchical ancilla-controlled equivariant quantum network architecture to limit trainable Lie-algebra growth and improve initialization trainability.
motivation: Equivariance in quantum neural networks provides an inductive bias but does not restrict the noncommuting closure of trainable generators, which can grow rapidly and hinder optimization.
method: The authors introduce commuting invariant-sector projectors on the data register that select parameterized operations on a shared ancilla register, confining noncommuting dynamics, and prove a group-independent bound on the trainable Lie-algebra dimension.
result: For constant ancilla dimension and layer-wise control modes, the bound is polynomial in data qubits, and finite-size simulations show slower gradient-variance decay and larger initialization gradients than conventional equivariant circuits.
conclusion: Restricting trainable Lie-algebra growth via hierarchical ancilla-controlled subspace projections is a structural strategy for initialization trainability in the studied regimes.

title: Encryptability As A Coordinate Choice: Depth-One Homomorphic Federated Learning Of Quantum Neural Networks
authors: Marcel Mordarski, Nathan Mani, Arshad Patel, William Knottenbelt, Roberto Bondesan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30581v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Encrypted training relies on keeping server-side updates low-degree. This constraint traditionally excludes models whose weights inhabit a compact Lie group (notably variational quantum circuits, where every trainable weight is an [MATH] rotation). Expressed in Euler angles or discrete alphabets, these updates appear transcendental, historically demanding prohibitive costs: one client--server round per gate, or upwards of [MATH] operations per weight. This penalty is strictly an artefact of coordinates. In the unit-quaternion (spin) chart, group composition is exactly bilinear (degree two, with coefficients in [MATH]). Consequently, encrypted rotation updates cost one multiplicative level and federated averaging costs zero in any levelled homomorphic scheme, completely eliminating bootstrapping. This implementation-independent algebraic property is confirmed across two cryptographic backends, introducing only [MATH] and [MATH] rad of aggregation error. Leveraging this reduction yields a non-interactive protocol for encrypted federated training of hybrid quantum--classical networks. It includes correctness proofs for aggregation and sign handling, plus a compilation lemma proving parameterised entanglers add only constant-factor overhead without altering the depth class. Empirically, a paired five-seed study confirms zero measurable utility tax ([MATH] MSE, [MATH]), and a noise-budget ablation falsifies the hypothesis that encryption noise regularises. These convergence trends replicate across datasets and scale to [MATH] clients. Finally, hardware validation on a [MATH]-qubit processor achieves [MATH] fidelity against a [MATH] unencrypted control.
tldr: The paper shows that expressing quantum neural network rotations in a unit-quaternion chart makes encrypted updates bilinear, enabling a depth-one homomorphic federated learning protocol with negligible overhead.
motivation: Encrypted training of variational quantum circuits is traditionally expensive because group-valued weights in standard coordinates lead to high-degree server-side updates, requiring many rounds or bootstrapping.
method: The authors reformulate rotation updates in the spin/quaternion chart to achieve exact bilinear (degree-two) group composition, design a non-interactive encrypted federated protocol, and prove correctness for aggregation and sign handling plus a compilation lemma for parameterized entanglers.
result: Experiments show zero measurable utility tax and the protocol scales to many clients; hardware validation on a 27-qubit processor achieves high fidelity against an unencrypted control, with a noise-budget ablation falsifying encryption-noise regularization.
conclusion: Coordinate choice is the key to efficient encrypted quantum machine learning, enabling practical privacy-preserving federated training of hybrid quantum-classical networks.

title: Room-temperature Quantum-sensing Molecular Crystals Grown In Minutes
authors: Madhur Parashar, Guangzhao Chen, Emanuel Druga, Liang Z. Tan, Jeffrey Reimer, Ashok Ajoy
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30899v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum sensing increasingly demands materials combining room-temperature optical spin addressability and coherent control with rapid, accessible fabrication. Yet semiconductor platforms require costly materials and specialized processing, while molecular systems often depend on bespoke synthesis or involved crystal growth. Here we apply microspacing in-air sublimation (MAS) to rapidly fabricate quantum-sensing materials within minutes. Microgram quantities of commercially available precursors crystallize on glass, in air and without vacuum or inert-gas handling. Monitored in situ, growth yields optically clear, stoichiometric single crystals of excellent quality, including plates and needles with intrinsic optical waveguiding. Donor-acceptor charge-transfer co-crystals pairing anthracene or biphenyl with tetracyanobenzene, together with localized-exciton pentacene:pentacenequinone (P:PQ), exhibit room-temperature optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR). Charge-transfer ODMR resonances reach linewidths below [MATH], consistent with motional narrowing of mobile triplet excitons, while P:PQ supports coherent ensemble spin control with [MATH]. Functionality across chemically and electronically distinct pairs establishes MAS as an accessible screen for molecular quantum-sensing materials, connecting molecular crystal engineering with low-cost, chemically tunable thin triplet-spin layers and waveguiding sensor geometries for quantum sensing and microscopy.
tldr: Microspacing in-air sublimation rapidly grows room-temperature molecular crystals that exhibit optically detected magnetic resonance and coherent spin control for quantum sensing.
motivation: Quantum sensing needs materials with room-temperature optical spin addressability and rapid, low-cost fabrication, but semiconductor platforms are expensive and molecular systems often require bespoke synthesis or slow crystal growth.
method: The authors apply microspacing in-air sublimation (MAS) to grow microgram-scale single crystals of charge-transfer co-crystals and pentacene:pentacenequinone in air, then characterize their optical and spin properties via in situ monitoring and room-temperature optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR).
result: The crystals show room-temperature ODMR with sub-megahertz linewidths consistent with motional narrowing of mobile triplet excitons, and P:PQ supports coherent ensemble spin control, with intrinsic optical waveguiding in plate and needle morphologies.
conclusion: MAS provides an accessible screening route for molecular quantum-sensing materials, connecting molecular crystal engineering to low-cost, chemically tunable thin triplet-spin layers and waveguiding sensor geometries for quantum sensing and microscopy.

title: When Can Quantum Extreme Learning Machines Replace Quantum Reservoirs?
authors: Markus Baumann, Gerhard Stenzel, Jonas Stein, Claudia Linnhoff-Popien
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31027v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum reservoir computers (QRCs) retain information from earlier inputs, whereas reset-window quantum extreme learning machines (QELMs) start afresh and receive only a recent input window. We establish when this window can replace the reservoir's memory. Under our stated assumptions and with exact expectation values, sufficiently expressive QELMs can reproduce reservoir outputs arbitrarily accurately as their windows grow precisely when the influence of the omitted past becomes uniformly negligible. However, longer windows do not always solve the problem. We construct a simple two-qubit reservoir that performs temporal recall exactly, while every fixed-window predictor faces the same positive worst-case error over unbounded delays, regardless of model capacity. Analytical benchmarks and simulations distinguish missing history from limited features and finite measurements. The central conclusion is simple: better representations can improve how available information is used, but cannot recover a past the model never receives.
tldr: Reset-window quantum extreme learning machines can match quantum reservoirs only when the omitted past influence is negligible, and fixed-window predictors cannot overcome unbounded delays.
motivation: To determine when a memoryless QELM with a finite input window can replace a QRC that retains information from earlier inputs.
method: Theoretical analysis under exact expectation values, constructing a two-qubit reservoir that performs temporal recall exactly, with analytical benchmarks and simulations.
result: Sufficiently expressive QELMs reproduce reservoir outputs as windows grow iff the influence of the omitted past becomes uniformly negligible; every fixed-window predictor faces a positive worst-case error over unbounded delays regardless of model capacity.
conclusion: Better representations can improve how available information is used, but they cannot recover a past that the model never receives.

title: Cofi-dqi: Curve-based Optimal Function Intersection Via Decoded Quantum Interferometry
authors: Julia Shapiro Gretchen L. Matthews
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31484v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In 2025, Jordan et al. introduced Decoded Quantum Interferometry (DQI), a quantum algorithm for combinatorial optimization based on decoding. They considered Reed-Solomon decoding and its associated optimization problem, called Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI), which may be viewed as a polynomial regression problem over a finite field. DQI exhibits provable speedups on certain problem instances and establishes a connection between decoding problems and optimization tasks. Leveraging the well-understood dual structure and decoding theory of algebraic geometry codes from other curve families, we introduce COFI: Curve-based Optimal Function Intersection. By considering two-point Hermitian codes, Suzuki codes, and extended norm-trace codes, we broaden the range of algebraic geometry codes used in DQI and identify families that offer further improvements over one-point Hermitian codes in the Hermitian Optimal Polynomial Intersection framework considered by Jordan and Gu. Depending on the family and parameter regime, these curves can reduce quantum resource requirements or increase the number of constraints that can be considered.
tldr: The paper introduces COFI, a curve-based optimal function intersection framework that extends decoded quantum interferometry using algebraic geometry codes to improve quantum optimization performance.
motivation: Decoded quantum interferometry connects decoding problems to combinatorial optimization, and existing work mainly used Reed-Solomon and one-point Hermitian codes; broader algebraic geometry code families may reduce quantum resource requirements or increase the number of constraints.
method: The authors generalize the optimal polynomial intersection problem to curve-based optimal function intersection and analyze two-point Hermitian codes, Suzuki codes, and extended norm-trace codes within the DQI framework.
result: Depending on the code family and parameter regime, these curves can reduce quantum resource requirements or increase the number of constraints compared with one-point Hermitian codes in the Hermitian OPI setting.
conclusion: Curve-based algebraic geometry codes expand the design space for DQI and can offer performance improvements, but the work remains a specialized quantum algorithm and coding-theory contribution rather than a direct advance in the researcher's core interests.

title: Modeling Quantum Neural Network Gradient With Reinforcement Learning
authors: Nhan Trong Luu, Duong Trung Luu, Nam Ngoc Pham, Thang Cong Truong
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31066v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training quantum neural networks (QNNs) on near-term hardware remains hampered by two compounding difficulties: the exponential vanishing of gradient variance known as the barren plateau, and the [MATH] time and memory cost of differentiating through an [MATH]-qubit, [MATH]-layer circuit. We propose RLQ-Grad, a reinforcement-learning-based optimizer in which a classical policy [MATH] (a spectrally-normalized PPO agent) learns to propose parameter updates directly, conditioned on the QNN's current parameters, loss, accuracy, and previous update. Because the surrogate gradient is emitted by a classical network rather than obtained by differentiating through the unitary [MATH], its variance is not constrained by the barren plateau concentration bound, and its cost scales with the number of trainable parameters rather than the Hilbert-space dimension. We prove these properties formally and verify them on a hardware-efficient ansatz across four supervised benchmarks with up to [MATH] qubits. RLQ-Grad preserves a near-flat gradient-variance curve where backpropagation, parameter-shift, and adjoint differentiation decay by 1 to 2 orders of magnitude. Accounting for the full training pipeline (PPO rollouts, actor-critic updates, and optimizer states), RLQ-Grad needs under 2 MB of memory and runs [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH] faster per iteration than these three methods at [MATH]. It improves top-1 accuracy by up to [MATH] over gradient-based baselines on circuits of up to 12 qubits, and matches dedicated barren plateau mitigation methods on CIFAR-10 at 14 to 20 qubits, where evolutionary and gradient-free optimizers collapse to chance.
tldr: RLQ-Grad uses a spectrally-normalized PPO policy to propose parameter updates for QNNs, avoiding barren-plateau-limited gradients and reducing differentiation cost.
motivation: Training quantum neural networks on near-term hardware is hampered by exponentially vanishing gradients (barren plateaus) and the high time and memory cost of differentiating through deep quantum circuits.
method: A classical reinforcement learning policy is trained to output parameter updates conditioned on the QNN's current parameters, loss, accuracy, and previous update, with formal proofs of variance and cost scaling.
result: Across supervised benchmarks up to 20 qubits, RLQ-Grad preserves a near-flat gradient-variance curve, uses under 2 MB of memory, runs faster per iteration than backpropagation, parameter-shift, and adjoint differentiation, and improves accuracy over gradient-based baselines.
conclusion: RL-based optimization can mitigate barren plateaus and reduce resource costs for QNN training, but the work is an applied quantum machine learning contribution without a clear information-theoretic advance.

title: A Search-to-decision Reduction For The Linear Code Equivalence Problem
authors: Jean-Fran\c{c}ois Biasse, Giacomo Micheli, Benjamin Prada, Philip Waitkevich
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31517v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a polynomial-time reduction from the search variant of the linear code equivalence problem (i.e. the search for a linear isometry between the inputs) to its decisional variant. More precisely, given two linearly equivalent codes [MATH], we show how to recover a linear isometry between them by making a polynomial number of queries to an oracle for decisional linear code equivalence. First, we prove that search-Permutation Code Equivalence (search-PCE -- the problem of finding a permutation [MATH] mapping [MATH] to [MATH]) reduces in polynomial time to PCE (i.e. the problem of deciding if there is a permutation map from [MATH] to [MATH]) via at most [MATH] oracle calls on instances of dimension [MATH] and length at most [MATH]. We then extend this approach to linearly equivalent codes: we recover the permutation part of a linear isometry via at most [MATH] calls to a Linear Code Equivalence (LCE) oracle on instances of the same size, and we give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm to recover the diagonal part once this permutation is known. Altogether, this yields a polynomial-time procedure to recover a linear isometry from an oracle for decisional LCE. From a linear-algebraic perspective, our results provide an explicit reconstruction of a monomial equivalence between two matrix representations from oracle access to the corresponding orbit membership problem.
tldr: The paper gives a polynomial-time search-to-decision reduction for the linear code equivalence problem, recovering a linear isometry from an oracle for decisional code equivalence.
motivation: Linear and permutation code equivalence underlie several post-quantum cryptographic proposals, and understanding the relationship between their search and decision variants is important for security analysis.
method: The authors first reduce search-PCE to PCE via polynomially many oracle calls, then extend the technique to linearly equivalent codes by recovering the permutation part through LCE oracle queries and deterministically reconstructing the diagonal part.
result: They obtain a polynomial-time procedure that recovers a full linear isometry between linearly equivalent codes from an oracle for decisional LCE, with explicit bounds on the number of queries.
conclusion: The reduction clarifies the complexity relationship between search and decision versions of code equivalence, with implications for the hardness assumptions used in post-quantum cryptography.

title: Peregrino: A Full-Hardware Accelerator For The Complete Falcon Post-Quantum Digital Signature Scheme On Resource-Constrained Edge Devices
authors: Antonio Carre\~no, Jaime Se\~nor, Jorge Portilla
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31252v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The arrival of quantum computers threatens the security guarantees of classical cryptography, since quantum algorithms can break schemes that remain secure against conventional attacks. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has therefore standardized a set of post-quantum cryptographic algorithms, among them Falcon, a lattice-based digital signature scheme with the most compact signature and public-key sizes of the standardized candidates. Falcon's reliance on floating-point arithmetic makes it hard to implement in hardware, and prior work offers only partial accelerators for specific operations such as signature generation or verification, or a single full implementation generated through high-level synthesis (HLS). This work presents Peregrino, the first hardware accelerator of the complete Falcon digital signature scheme designed from scratch in HDL, targeting resource-constrained edge devices without a native floating-point unit through an emulated floating-point datapath. Implemented on a single Artix 7 XC7A200T FPGA, Peregrino uses 85261 LUTs, 41382 FFs, 44 BRAMs, and 142 DSPs for the Falcon-1024 variant. Against the only prior full implementation, the HLS-based FalconTakesOff, it uses 1,9[MATH] fewer LUTs, 3,4[MATH] fewer FFs, 2,7[MATH] fewer BRAMs, and 9,9[MATH] fewer DSPs, fitting the entire scheme on one FPGA where the HLS design requires at least two. Operating as a peripheral of an on-chip MicroBlaze soft-core, the accelerator additionally reduces key-pair generation, signature generation, and signature verification clock cycles by 92\%, 96\%, and 85\% over the emulated floating-point reference software.
tldr: Peregrino is the first full-hardware accelerator for the complete Falcon post-quantum digital signature scheme, implemented on a resource-constrained FPGA with an emulated floating-point datapath.
motivation: Quantum computers threaten classical cryptography, and NIST has standardized Falcon as a compact lattice-based signature scheme, but its floating-point arithmetic makes efficient hardware implementation difficult, especially for edge devices without native floating-point units.
method: The authors designed Peregrino from scratch in HDL, using an emulated floating-point datapath on a single Artix 7 XC7A200T FPGA, and integrated it as a peripheral to an on-chip MicroBlaze soft-core processor.
result: Peregrino uses 85,261 LUTs, 41,382 FFs, 44 BRAMs, and 142 DSPs for Falcon-1024, reducing resource usage by factors of 1.9x–9.9x compared to the HLS-based FalconTakesOff, and reducing key-pair generation, signature generation, and verification clock cycles by 92%, 96%, and 85% over the emulated floating-point reference software.
conclusion: Peregrino enables the complete Falcon signature scheme on a single FPGA for edge devices, advancing practical post-quantum cryptography deployment, but it is a hardware engineering contribution rather than an information-theoretic or quantum-foundational result.

title: How To Break The Miranda Signature Scheme Over Matrix Gabidulin Codes
authors: Adrien Vin\c{c}otte
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Miranda signature scheme relies on masking a matrix code which disposes of a masked underlying structure, and the knowledge of which allows for efficient error decoding. We consider a Gabidulin code which is expanded into a matrix code, that is only \Fq-linear. An additional masking is then applied to it. The attack proposed here shares similarities with that of [Le26, [URL] on the EGMC encryption scheme, which also follows the paradigm described above. It consists in recovering the Fqm-linear structure of a masked matrix Gabidulin code by reducing to a MinRank instance to be solved over the extension field Fqm, but where the matrices have coefficients in Fq. Such an instance can be efficiently solved. However, unlike the previous attack, it is possible to reduce in polynomial time to such a MinRank instance in the case of the Miranda signature scheme. This results in a particularly efficient key recovery attack against the parameters proposed for Miranda. For example, for the proposed parameter set with m=79, the complexity drops from 146 bits to 46 bits in this attack.
tldr: The paper presents an efficient key-recovery attack on the Miranda signature scheme by exploiting the hidden Fqm-linear structure of a masked matrix Gabidulin code via a polynomial-time reduction to a MinRank instance.
motivation: Miranda is a code-based post-quantum signature scheme whose security rests on the hardness of recovering the masked matrix-code structure, and its proposed parameters must be validated against structural attacks.
method: The attack recovers the Fqm-linear structure of the masked matrix Gabidulin code by reducing it, in polynomial time, to a MinRank problem over the extension field Fqm whose matrices have entries in Fq, which can then be solved efficiently.
result: For the proposed parameter set with m=79, the attack lowers the complexity of breaking Miranda from 146 bits to 46 bits, demonstrating a severe security loss.
conclusion: The proposed Miranda parameters are insecure, and the scheme requires substantial redesign or parameter adjustment to resist this structural MinRank-based key-recovery attack.

title: Representation-Aware Transport-Information Measure For Non-inclusive Discrete Supports
authors: Koretaka Yuge
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Information-theoretic measures for comparing probability distributions are widely used across physics and other fields. When two discrete distributions have non-inclusive supports, however, the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence is in general not directly applicable, and various alternative divergences and distances have been introduced. These measures compare the resulting distributions themselves, but do not generally retain information about the representation transformations by which the discrete distributions are generated from underlying continuous ones. Here we introduce a representation-aware transport-information measure for discrete distributions with non-inclusive supports, formulated based on the standard KL divergence. We consider two continuous reference distributions, each transformed into a discrete representation through its own discretization scheme. Rather than comparing only the resulting discrete distributions or their continuous references, we additionally retain local information associated with the representation-change schemes. The resulting measure can therefore distinguish discrete representations that may have identical discrete probability landscapes but originate from different continuous references or discretization schemes. The construction is based on the transport-information cost of continuous-to-discrete representation in the framework of unavoidable canonical nonlinearity (UCN). UCN provides a non-arbitrary correspondence between the transport cost of discretization as an extrinsic geometric operation and the information-theoretic indistinguishability of nearby continuous distributions, thereby allowing a discrete representation to be associated with a local family of underlying continuous distributions on the statistical manifold.
tldr: The paper introduces a representation-aware transport-information measure for comparing discrete distributions with non-inclusive supports, retaining information about the continuous-to-discrete representation schemes.
motivation: Standard divergences like Kullback-Leibler fail for non-inclusive supports and ignore how discrete distributions arise from continuous references, so a measure is needed that accounts for representation transformations.
method: The authors formulate the measure using the standard Kullback-Leibler divergence and the transport-information cost of continuous-to-discrete representation within the framework of unavoidable canonical nonlinearity (UCN).
result: The resulting measure can distinguish discrete representations that have identical discrete probability landscapes but originate from different continuous references or discretization schemes.
conclusion: This provides a non-arbitrary correspondence between discretization transport cost and information-theoretic indistinguishability, linking discrete representations to local families of continuous distributions on the statistical manifold.

title: Optimal Noisy Sequential Multiparameter Quantum Sensing
authors: Andrew Tanggara, Lorc\'an O Conlon, Alexey V. Gorshkov, Kishor Bharti
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30398v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The most general strategy for estimating parameters of a quantum channel is to probe the channel many times sequentially with the help of coherent ancillary systems. However, finding the strategy that minimizes the mean-squared error (MSE) is a notoriously hard problem, requiring optimization over the initial probe state, intermediate evolutions, final measurement, and classical postprocessing. In this work, we study how the minimum attainable MSE can be bounded from below in this setting. We propose a lower bound for the MSE of any physically implementable sequential sensing strategy that applies to estimating parameters of any physical quantum evolution, including quantum channels probed over multiple time steps under temporally correlated noise and general temporally correlated quantum processes. We show that this lower bound can be formulated as a semidefinite program (SDP).
