Our bound generalizes the Nagaoka-Hayashi lower bound (that applies to parameter estimation tasks with separable measurements) to the regime where the quantum channel can be accessed sequentially multiple times. For regular finite-dimensional single-parameter sequential estimation tasks admitting an optimal strategy, we show that our SDP bound is tight and provide a procedure to obtain a locally optimal strategy from the SDP optimizer. Using our optimization bound, we compute the MSE lower bound and derive new protocols for several other physically motivated problems including error-corrected quantum sensing under an unknown correlated noise model, multiparameter estimation, and estimation with qudit systems.
tldr: The paper proposes an SDP-computable lower bound on mean-squared error for sequential multiparameter quantum sensing under correlated noise, generalizing the Nagaoka-Hayashi bound and yielding optimal strategies in some cases.
motivation: Finding optimal sequential quantum sensing strategies is notoriously hard because one must optimize over probe states, intermediate evolutions, measurements, and classical postprocessing. Lower bounds provide benchmarks and guide protocol design.
method: It formulates a semidefinite program (SDP) lower bound for any physically implementable sequential strategy estimating parameters of arbitrary quantum evolutions, including channels probed over multiple time steps under temporally correlated noise and general correlated processes. The bound generalizes the Nagaoka-Hayashi bound to sequential channel access.
result: For regular finite-dimensional single-parameter sequential estimation tasks admitting an optimal strategy, the SDP bound is tight and a locally optimal strategy can be obtained from the SDP optimizer. Applications include error-corrected quantum sensing under unknown correlated noise, multiparameter estimation, and qudit systems.
conclusion: The work provides a practical SDP framework for benchmarking and designing noisy sequential quantum sensing protocols, with extensions to multiparameter and error-corrected settings.

title: Construction Of Partial Join Graphs With Perfect State Transfer In Shunt Decomposition-Based Quantum Walks
authors: Banita Katuwal, Y Lakshmi Naidu, Srinath M S, Supriyo Dutta
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30490v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we define directed partial join graphs with signed couplings and construct discrete-time quantum-walk transition operators for these graphs using the shunt-decomposition framework. The resulting transition operators apply to several important graph families, including complete graphs with loops, circulant partial joins, complete bipartite graphs, tensor powers of complete bipartite graphs, all with signed couplings. For each family, we identify the corresponding structure of the transition operator and derive necessary and sufficient conditions for periodicity and perfect state transfer (PST), when one of the two directed regular graphs admits PST. Based on these results, we identify two types of state transfer; internal PST, which occurs between vertices within the same graph, and coupling PST, which occurs between two components of join graphs. We further develop a double-cover construction for directed partial join graphs and derive conditions for periodicity and PST when the associated transition operators do not necessarily commute. Using this construction, we establish PST results for double covers of complete graphs with loops. In particular, we provide an example in which the complete graph \(K_n\) does not exhibit PST for \(n\geq4\), whereas a suitable partial join of \(K_n\) exhibits PST when \(n=2^m\), \(m\geq2\). Hence, these results extend the class of graph families admitting PST in shunt-decomposition-based quantum walks and provide a unified framework for studying quantum state transfer in graph joins, products, and covers.
tldr: The paper constructs directed partial join graphs and derives conditions for perfect state transfer in shunt-decomposition-based discrete-time quantum walks.
motivation: Perfect state transfer in quantum walks is a fundamental primitive for quantum information transfer, and graph joins provide a versatile framework for designing networks with desirable transfer properties.
method: Defines directed partial join graphs with signed couplings and constructs discrete-time quantum-walk transition operators via shunt decomposition; derives necessary and sufficient conditions for periodicity and PST for several graph families, and introduces a double-cover construction.
result: Identifies internal and coupling PST, establishes conditions for PST when one component admits PST, and shows that although K_n lacks PST for n≥4, a suitable partial join of K_n exhibits PST for n=2^m, m≥2.
conclusion: The results extend the class of graphs admitting PST in shunt-decomposition quantum walks and offer a unified framework for analyzing state transfer in graph joins, products, and covers.

title: Disentangling Expressibility, Symmetry Protection, And Hardware Noise In Variational Quantum Simulation Of The Two-Flavor Schwinger Model
authors: Karthikeya Machiraju, Krishna Sujith, Kaustav Bhowmick
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30496v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing quantum simulations of the two-flavor Schwinger model have run at a single lattice size, and it is not known how far the variational approach can be pushed or which weakness stops it first. Following the model from N = 2 to 6 staggered lattice sites, we find that the binding constraint at reachable sizes is hardware noise rather than circuit expressibility or trainability, and identify N = 3 as the immediately viable extension of existing trapped-ion experiments. The energy error of a charge-conserving ansatz collapses onto one function of p/d, the ratio of variational parameters to physical-sector dimension, and falls by more than two orders of magnitude as p/d rises through order unity, giving the expressibility condition L(4N - 1) >= binom(2N,N) for L circuit layers. The condition is local in chemical potential: at N = 3 the layer count sufficient at zero chemical potential leaves a 74.38% error near the first-order boundary, while one further layer reaches 0.08%. Charge conservation also protects trainability and prevents charge-sector leakage: as the qubit count doubles from 4 to 8, the normalized gradient variance falls to 1/3.56 of its starting value for the constrained ansatz, versus 1/13.57 for an unconstrained circuit. Comparing a global contraction with per-gate local noise, a fixed-parameter control shows that the noise model, not whether the optimizer runs inside the noisy loop, sets how strongly noise degrades the first-order transition. At N = 4, a noiseless control reaches 0.12% mean error, whereas the same circuit at 1.00% depolarizing noise reaches 25.69 to 52.81%.
tldr: Hardware noise, not circuit expressibility or trainability, is the binding constraint in variational quantum simulation of the two-flavor Schwinger model at reachable lattice sizes, with N = 3 identified as the immediately viable extension.
motivation: Existing quantum simulations of the two-flavor Schwinger model use only a single lattice size, so it is unclear how far the variational approach can be pushed and which limitation appears first.
method: The authors simulate the two-flavor Schwinger model from N = 2 to 6 staggered lattice sites using a charge-conserving variational ansatz, varying circuit depth and chemical potential, and comparing constrained versus unconstrained circuits as well as global versus per-gate noise models.
result: The energy error collapses onto a function of p/d (variational parameters over physical-sector dimension), yielding the expressibility condition L(4N - 1) >= binom(2N,N); at N = 3, one extra layer reduces error from 74.38% to 0.08%, charge conservation slows gradient-variance decay, and at N = 4 a noiseless control reaches 0.12% mean error versus 25.69–52.81% under 1% depolarizing noise.
conclusion: At accessible system sizes, hardware noise limits variational simulation more than expressibility or trainability, while symmetry protection helps trainability; N = 3 is the most promising near-term extension of trapped-ion experiments.

title: Computational Aberration-retrieval With Entangled Photons
authors: Baptiste Courme, Yoonseok Baek, Hugo Defienne
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31049v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adaptive optics (AO) is central to high-resolution microscopy, yet conventional implementations often require repeated correction-and-measurement cycles whose number increases with aberration complexity. This measurement burden can become prohibitive when the available temporal window for correction is short or when photon budgets are constrained. Here, we demonstrate an AO strategy that exploits the spatial correlations of entangled photon pairs to retrieve aberrations directly. By using the second-order correlation function as an aberration-sensitive metric, the required correction can be determined with only a few measurements, without relying on image-based feedback or iterative optimization. This correlation-based approach establishes an efficient framework for AO leveraging quantum light, offering a new route toward quantum-enhanced microscopy in regimes where conventional correction strategies become challenging.
tldr: The paper demonstrates adaptive optics using spatial correlations of entangled photon pairs to retrieve aberrations with few measurements, enabling quantum-enhanced microscopy.
motivation: Conventional adaptive optics requires many correction-and-measurement cycles, especially for complex aberrations, which is impractical when photon budgets are low or correction time is short.
method: The authors use the second-order correlation function of entangled photon pairs as an aberration-sensitive metric to directly determine the required correction, avoiding iterative feedback and image-based optimization.
result: The correlation-based approach retrieves aberrations with only a few measurements, significantly reducing the measurement burden compared to conventional adaptive optics.
conclusion: This work establishes an efficient framework for adaptive optics using quantum light, offering a route toward quantum-enhanced microscopy in photon-starved or time-constrained regimes.

title: Critical Escape Dynamics Of An Active Particle Moving On Curved Surfaces
authors: Maxim Root, Hartmut L\"owen, Peter Sollich, Lorenzo Caprini, Alexander P. Antonov
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30455v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On the macroscopic scale, active (self-propelled) objects moving through complex environments are often subject to effects arising from both the curvature of the surrounding surface and external influences such as gravity. We study the Kramers escape problem for active Brownian particles in two settings: motion in an external potential driven solely by gradient forces, and motion on a curved manifold subject to an additional constant gravitational force. In the absence of translational noise, a sharp dynamical transition occurs when the self-propulsion velocity [MATH] reaches a critical velocity [MATH] required for an escape. Above this threshold, the escape rate [MATH] follows a universal scaling form, [MATH], with an exponent [MATH] for the escape in a potential and [MATH] for the escape on a curved manifold in the presence of gravity. These distinct exponents reveal how the interplay of activity, surface curvature, and gravity determines the critical escape dynamics. Our theoretical predictions are verified by numerical simulations.
tldr: The paper studies Kramers escape dynamics for active Brownian particles in external potentials and on curved surfaces with gravity, finding universal scaling and distinct critical exponents.
motivation: Active particles in complex environments experience curvature and gravity, but how these factors affect escape from metastable states is not fully understood.
method: The authors analytically solve the Kramers escape problem for active Brownian particles without translational noise, considering gradient forces and motion on a curved manifold with constant gravity, and validate with numerical simulations.
result: They identify a sharp dynamical transition at a critical self-propulsion velocity; above it, the escape rate follows a universal scaling law with exponent 1/2 in a potential and a different exponent on a curved manifold with gravity.
conclusion: The distinct exponents demonstrate how activity, surface curvature, and gravity jointly determine critical escape dynamics, offering a framework for active matter in complex geometries.

title: The para--Racah Hamiltonian As An Exactly Solvable Discretization Of The P\"oschl--Teller Box
authors: St\'ephane Z. Beaulac, Nicolas Cramp\'e, Quentin Labriet, Lucia Morey, Marlon Josue Rivera Valladares, Luc Vinet
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30624v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The para--Racah Hamiltonian is the Jacobi matrix [MATH] of the para--Racah polynomials, taken at the persymmetric value of their isospectral deformation parameter: a mirror--symmetric tridiagonal matrix whose spectrum is a bi--lattice, the squares [MATH] and [MATH] of two interlaced arithmetic progressions of unit step, and which carries out fractional revival when the grid parameters [MATH] and [MATH] satisfy a Diophantine condition. As the number of sites grows, [MATH] contracts to the trigonometric Hamiltonian on a finite interval. We establish this twice: on the recurrence relation, and on the polynomials themselves, for which it is the confluence Racah~[MATH]~Jacobi. Both grid parameters survive: [MATH] becomes a scalar centrifugal term at the interior point fixed by the mirror --- the exact analogue of the para--Krawtchouk origin --- while [MATH] sets two confining singular walls at the ends, which turn the spectrum into the quadratic pair [MATH] with Jacobi eigenfunctions [MATH], the two sublattices converging to two families that differ only by the sign of the second Jacobi parameter. The mirror symmetry of [MATH] becomes the reflection about the midpoint; it grades the two families and carries the fractional revival to the limit. Algebraically, the bispectral pair of the discrete model, which generates the Racah algebra [MATH], becomes a pair of generators of the Jacobi algebra [MATH] --- one rung down the Askey--Wilson hierarchy --- the dynamical algebra of the P\"oschl--Teller Hamiltonian.
tldr: The paper shows that the para-Racah Hamiltonian, a persymmetric Jacobi matrix, contracts to the trigonometric Pöschl-Teller Hamiltonian as the number of sites grows, connecting Racah and Jacobi algebras.
motivation: To understand how discrete orthogonal polynomial models with fractional revival relate to continuous exactly solvable quantum systems and how algebraic structures deform under contraction.
method: They analyze the Jacobi matrix of para-Racah polynomials and take a large-site limit both on the recurrence relation and on the polynomials themselves, identifying the confluence Racah to Jacobi.
result: The limit produces two sublattices with Jacobi eigenfunctions, two confining singular walls, and a mirror-symmetric grading, while the Racah algebra contracts to the Jacobi algebra.
conclusion: The para-Racah Hamiltonian provides an exactly solvable discretization of the Pöschl-Teller box, bridging discrete and continuous algebraic structures and preserving fractional revival in the limit.

title: Recent Advances In Poled Lithium Niobate
authors: Kibret A. Messalea, Tim Weiss, Yang Yang, Hamed Arianfard, Brett C. Johnson, Alberto Peruzzo
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30736v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lithium niobate is a versatile material for both classical and quantum photonics, recognized for its outstanding electro-optic and nonlinear optical properties. Through a process known as poling, periodic ferroelectric crystal domains can be engineered to enable quasi-phase-matched frequency conversion, efficient modulation, and the generation of quantum light sources. The emergence of lithium niobate on insulator technology has further enhanced its suitability for scalable integrated photonics, offering ultra-low optical losses and strong light confinement while retaining the material's inherent advantages. Here, the techniques used to fabricate and characterize periodically poled lithium niobate are reviewed. Key developments are discussed, offering insights into the future of domain engineering of lithium niobate.
tldr: A review of fabrication and characterization techniques for periodically poled lithium niobate, a material platform for classical and quantum photonics.
motivation: Lithium niobate offers strong electro-optic and nonlinear optical properties, and poling enables quasi-phase-matched frequency conversion, efficient modulation, and quantum light sources. Lithium niobate on insulator further enables scalable integrated photonics with low loss and strong confinement.
method: The paper reviews techniques used to fabricate and characterize periodically poled lithium niobate and discusses key developments in domain engineering.
result: It summarizes advances in poling and characterization, highlighting the suitability of lithium niobate on insulator for scalable integrated photonics and quantum light generation.
conclusion: The review offers insights into future directions for domain engineering of lithium niobate, but it is a materials and photonics review rather than a direct contribution to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Quantum-circuit Simulation Of Three-flavor Neutrino Oscillations: Vacuum, Matter, And Cp Diagnostics
authors: Daming Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30875v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We simulate three-flavor neutrino oscillations on two-qubit quantum circuits. The flavor space is embedded as [MATH], [MATH], [MATH] with the [MATH] channel kept inert, and the input mixing parameters (NuFIT~5.3, normal ordering) follow the global fit. We verify three physical settings against analytic or exact references: vacuum propagation, reproduced by a mass-eigenstate phase circuit to [MATH]; constant-density Mikheev--Smirnov--Wolfenstein (MSW) matter effects, showing resonant flavor conversion when the matter potential [MATH] crosses [MATH]; and varying-density (supernova shock-shell) propagation by slicing plus second-order Suzuki--Trotter splitting, agreeing with exact evolution to [MATH]. We report a Suzuki--Trotter precision--resource calibration varying order, step number, and matrix/probability error. It delimits brute-force Trotterization on solar baselines: we quantify both standard alternatives, coherence averaging and adiabatic MSW. We also compute quantum-information diagnostics from the same model parameters, namely mode entanglement and the CP asymmetry. Finally, we extend the framework to open quantum systems via a Lindblad master equation with dephasing and absorptive channels. These results provide a reproducible link between low-energy oscillation observables and quantum-information measures.
tldr: Simulates three-flavor neutrino oscillations on two-qubit quantum circuits, covering vacuum, matter, and CP diagnostics, with Suzuki-Trotter calibration and Lindblad open-system extensions.
motivation: To connect low-energy neutrino oscillation observables with quantum-information measures and explore quantum-circuit simulation of particle-physics phenomena.
method: Embeds three-flavor neutrino states in two-qubit circuits with one flavor inert, uses NuFIT parameters and Suzuki-Trotter splitting for varying density, and computes entanglement and CP asymmetry; extends to Lindblad dephasing and absorption.
result: Reproduces vacuum and MSW matter effects to high precision, calibrates Trotter precision-resource tradeoffs, and quantifies alternatives like coherence averaging and adiabatic MSW for solar baselines.
conclusion: Provides a reproducible quantum-circuit framework linking neutrino oscillations to quantum-information diagnostics, though it does not advance core quantum information theory.

title: Interpolating Walk Between Discrete-time Quantum Walk And Its Intrinsic Random Walk On Graph
authors: Yusuke Higuchi, Etsuo Segawa, Honoka Shiratori, Saori Yoshino
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30931v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider an interpolation with the parameter [MATH] between the discrete-time quantum ([MATH]) and its intrinsic random ([MATH]) walks on a finite connected graph. Its time evolution is defined by the convex combination of the Kraus (CPTP) maps of the quantum and random walks. The Kraus map of the random walk is represented by taking a kind of projection of that of the quantum walk. The time evolution of the interpolation is interpreted as the combination of the following two dynamics of [MATH] walkers on the same graph correlated with each other: [MATH] walkers move independently of each other (no-correlation) with probability [MATH], while [MATH] walkers always move into the same position (the maximal correlation) with probability [MATH] at each time step. In this paper, we generalize the random walk to a new walk, namely, the correlated walk, which preserves the intrinsic property and relaxes the maximal correlation of the random walk. This correlation is determined by a partition of the arc sets in the underlying graph. We show that the eigenvalues of the interpolating walk between the correlated and quantum walks live in [MATH] and that the absorption state coincides with that of the correlated walk, which is characterized by the underlying graph structures.
tldr: The paper introduces an interpolation between discrete-time quantum walks and an intrinsic random walk on a graph via convex combinations of Kraus maps, generalizing to a correlated walk and analyzing its eigenvalues and absorption state.
motivation: To understand the transition between quantum and classical random walks and to characterize correlations that preserve intrinsic graph properties.
method: The time evolution is defined as a convex combination of Kraus (CPTP) maps for the quantum and random walks, where the random walk map is a projection of the quantum walk map; the random walk is generalized to a correlated walk determined by a partition of the arc sets.
result: The eigenvalues of the interpolating walk between the correlated and quantum walks are shown to lie in a specific interval, and the absorption state coincides with that of the correlated walk, characterized by the underlying graph structures.
conclusion: The work provides a framework linking quantum walks and correlated walks, showing that spectral and absorption properties are governed by graph partitions.

title: Highly Scalable Selectorless Cryogenic Memory Array Using Ferroelectric Josephson Field-Effect Transistors
authors: Shamiul Alam Saheeb Ahmad
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30672v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scalable memory systems that satisfy the temperature, speed, and energy requirements of cryogenic environments are essential for the development of large-scale quantum computers. They may also benefit high-performance computing and space applications. However, existing cryogenic memory technologies often suffer from limited scalability, low operating speed, and/or high power consumption, restricting the scalability of target applications. Ferroelectric Josephson field-effect transistors (Fe-JoFETs), which combine ferroelectric polarization with the superconducting properties of Josephson junctions, offer a promising solution. The ferroelectric layer enables nonvolatile storage capability, while the Josephson junction supports high-speed, energy-efficient operations. In this work, we leverage Fe-JoFETs to develop a highly scalable, ultra-low-power, nonvolatile cryogenic memory array that does not need additional selector devices for random access. Moreover, the superconducting component of Fe-JoFET provides a binary decision during read, eliminating the need for sensing peripheral circuitry. We first develop a physics-based Verilog-A compact model for Fe-JoFETs and use it to verify the functionality of the proposed memory array. By eliminating both selector and sensing circuitry, the proposed memory architecture offers higher scalability than existing technologies. The ultra-low-power operation of this memory also makes it compatible with strict power budgets of cryogenic applications.
tldr: A selectorless cryogenic memory array based on ferroelectric Josephson field-effect transistors is proposed for scalable quantum computing hardware.
motivation: Large-scale quantum computers require cryogenic memory with high scalability, speed, and low power, but existing technologies struggle to meet these demands.
method: A physics-based Verilog-A compact model for Fe-JoFETs is developed and used to verify a memory array that eliminates selector and sensing circuitry.
result: The architecture offers higher scalability and ultra-low-power nonvolatile operation compatible with cryogenic power budgets.
conclusion: Fe-JoFET-based memory could enable scalable cryogenic memory for quantum computing and other cryogenic applications.

title: Fundamental Limits Of Sequence Reconstruction Problems In Immunogenomics
authors: Jaswanthi Mandalapu, Deepak Charan, V. Arvind Rameshwar, Nir Weinberger
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31501v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The goal of personalized immunogenomics is to recover an individual's germline immunoglobulin gene segments from 'repertoire sequences' altered by trimming, extension, and mutation. In this work, we study the fundamental trace complexity (or the number of samples/traces required for accurate reconstruction) of D-gene reconstruction under three biologically motivated trace-generation models introduced by Bhardwaj et al. (2021) and develop practical algorithms for reconstruction problems left open in the original work. First, for the TrimSuffixAndExtend model, we establish the optimal trace complexity to be {\Theta(n)}, and develop a low-complexity Prefix-Filtered Mode (PFM) decoder that achieves this scaling. Second, for the closely related two-sided TrimAndExtend model, we show that the optimal trace complexity is instead {\Theta(n^2)}, and is achieved by the simple Bit-Wise Mode (BWM) decoder. Third, for the SuffixExtend-t(TrimSuffix) model, we establish polynomially separated lower and upper bounds on trace complexity. Our results follow from information-theoretic lower bounds coupled with tight analyses of the proposed reconstruction algorithms.
tldr: This paper studies the fundamental trace complexity of D-gene reconstruction in immunogenomics under three biologically motivated trace-generation models and develops practical reconstruction algorithms.
motivation: Personalized immunogenomics aims to recover germline immunoglobulin gene segments from repertoire sequences altered by trimming, extension, and mutation, but the fundamental sample complexity of this reconstruction problem was left open for several models.
method: The authors derive information-theoretic lower bounds on trace complexity and analyze low-complexity decoders, including a Prefix-Filtered Mode decoder and a Bit-Wise Mode decoder, for the TrimSuffixAndExtend, TrimAndExtend, and SuffixExtend-t(TrimSuffix) models.
result: They establish optimal trace complexity of Θ(n) for TrimSuffixAndExtend, Θ(n^2) for TrimAndExtend, and polynomially separated lower and upper bounds for SuffixExtend-t(TrimSuffix).
conclusion: The work resolves open reconstruction problems from Bhardwaj et al. (2021) by providing tight or improved complexity characterizations and practical algorithms for immunogenomic sequence reconstruction.

title: Unified Description Of Random Motions And Generalized Fokker-Planck Equations
authors: Luca Angelani
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30424v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This review surveys diverse types of random motion within a unified framework, introducing essential mathematical tools, including special functions and fractional calculus, in a pedagogical manner. We focus on generalized random motions in one-dimensional space described by Fokker-Planck like equations, whose fundamental solutions take a universal and simple form in the Laplace-Fourier domain in terms of a generic function [MATH]. By exploring the functional forms of [MATH] consistent with physical constraints, we derive a broad class of stochastic dynamics. This includes Brownian and active motion, simple and anomalous diffusion, and processes featuring stochastic resetting or trapping mechanisms. For each case, we provide the corresponding kinetic equation, explicit solutions (where available), and mean-square displacements alongside their asymptotic behaviors. Finally, we discuss the physical interpretation of these motions through the lens of time-changed processes and subordinators.
tldr: A pedagogical review that unifies diverse random motions through generalized Fokker-Planck equations and fractional calculus, covering Brownian, active, anomalous diffusion, resetting, and trapping.
motivation: To provide a unified mathematical framework for different types of stochastic motion that often appear in separate contexts.
method: Exploits a universal form of fundamental solutions in the Laplace-Fourier domain and explores admissible functional forms of a generic function to derive a broad class of stochastic dynamics.
result: Derives kinetic equations, explicit solutions where available, and mean-square displacements with asymptotic behaviors for many processes, including anomalous diffusion and stochastic resetting.
conclusion: Interprets the motions via time-changed processes and subordinators, offering a coherent picture of generalized random motion.

title: Solving Graph Coloring Problems Using Feedback-Based Algorithm For Quantum Optimization
authors: Yuika Kawatomi, Yukina Tatsuta, Kazue Kudo
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30991v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The feedback-based algorithm for quantum optimization (FALQON), which is an extension of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA), is a promising approach for finding approximate solutions to combinatorial optimization problems. The FALQON avoids the optimization of variational parameters by using information derived from iterative measurements. To solve a constrained combinatorial optimization problem, it is sometimes more efficient to use an XY mixer rather than the conventional X mixer. We applied the FALQON with the XY mixer to graph coloring and investigated the expectation value of the problem Hamiltonian, success probability of graph coloring, and fair sampling for several small-scale problems. The FALQON with the XY mixer exhibited better performance than that with the X mixer.
tldr: The paper applies the feedback-based algorithm for quantum optimization (FALQON) with an XY mixer to solve graph coloring problems on small instances.
motivation: Constrained combinatorial optimization problems are often better handled with XY mixers than the conventional X mixer, and FALQON avoids variational parameter optimization by using iteratively measured feedback.
method: FALQON, an extension of QAOA, is combined with an XY mixer and benchmarked against the X mixer variant on several small-scale graph coloring instances.
result: The XY-mixer FALQON outperforms the X-mixer version, as evaluated by the expectation value of the problem Hamiltonian, graph-coloring success probability, and fair sampling.
conclusion: XY mixers can improve FALQON's performance on constrained optimization problems such as graph coloring, though only small-scale demonstrations are provided.

title: Single-shot Coherent Process Tomography And Mid-infrared Polarimetry With Undetected Photons
authors: Marthe Zeja, Wen-Zhe Yan, Zhibo Hou, Sven Ramelow
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Measurements with undetected photons infer properties of a probe beam that is never detected, transferring mid-infrared information onto silicon-friendly wavelengths. Tomography in this paradigm has so far relied on switched settings or scanned phases, referenced across a drift-sensitive campaign; no protocol reads all Jones parameters from one frame. We show that a folded nonlinear interferometer with a diagonally pumped crossed-crystal source performs coherent process tomography of the undetected beam in a single spectrometer frame: it reconstructs all seven parameters of the beam's round-trip Jones matrix, the coherent part of the channel. Birefringent group-delay walk-off, normally a calibration nuisance, acts as a frequency multiplexer: each Jones-matrix element is assigned its own carrier, a spectral fringe period paired with a detector port. Because the multiplexing exploits the down-conversion bandwidth rather than merely tolerating it, a single Fourier transform per detector trace returns all four moduli and all three relative phases across that bandwidth, i.e., the full round-trip Jones spectrum up to a global phase, with no scan or setting change (after a one-time reference frame). Simultaneity makes every relative phase immune to common-mode drift, and a dark carrier, a self-interference term that unitarity forces to vanish, provides a built-in null test. For realistic parameters of a periodically poled KTP source the scheme yields wavelength-resolved mid-infrared polarimetry across 3.5-4.2 microns (~80 spectral points per Jones element) on a silicon camera, extending to depth-resolved Jones matrices, i.e., polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography with undetected photons. A Fisher-information analysis, the first we are aware of in undetected-photon tomography, sets the precision budget and compares delay multiplexing to sequential protocols at equal photon number.
tldr: A single-shot coherent process tomography scheme using undetected photons reconstructs the full round-trip Jones matrix of a mid-infrared probe beam from one spectrometer frame.
motivation: Existing tomography with undetected photons relies on switched settings or scanned phases, making it drift-sensitive and unable to read all Jones parameters from a single frame.
method: A folded nonlinear interferometer with a diagonally pumped crossed-crystal source exploits birefringent group-delay walk-off as a frequency multiplexer, assigning each Jones-matrix element a distinct carrier and extracting all parameters via a Fourier transform per detector trace.
result: The scheme reconstructs all seven parameters of the round-trip Jones matrix in a single frame, yielding wavelength-resolved mid-infrared polarimetry across 3.5–4.2 µm (~80 spectral points per Jones element) on a silicon camera, with a Fisher-information analysis comparing delay multiplexing to sequential protocols.
conclusion: The work enables drift-immune, single-shot mid-infrared polarimetry and extends to depth-resolved Jones matrices, offering a precision budget for undetected-photon tomography.

title: The Renormalization Group For A Slab Model Of The Spin Reorientation Transition
authors: D. Pescia
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31064v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In 1975, Polyakov invented a renormalization group algorithm for treating the problem of a classical isotropic planar Heisenberg ferromagnet. Here we define a tool - "parallel transport of frames" - that extends Polyakov's original renormalization group method to local magnetic anisotropies and, most significantly, the non-local dipolar interaction. We apply this tool to the problem of the spin reorientation transition in an ultrathin ferromagnetic slab with finite thickness. We find that integrating out the short wavelength spin wave fluctuations generates two local anisotropies that are absent from the microscopic dipolar energy Hamiltonian. Taking them into account yields the correct topology of the spin reorientation transition line, as observed experimentally and in numerical simulations.
tldr: The paper extends Polyakov's renormalization group method via a 'parallel transport of frames' tool to treat local magnetic anisotropies and non-local dipolar interactions in an ultrathin ferromagnetic slab, correctly reproducing the topology of the spin reorientation transition line.
motivation: Polyakov's original RG algorithm was designed for the classical isotropic planar Heisenberg ferromagnet and does not handle local anisotropies or the non-local dipolar interaction, which are essential for describing real magnetic slabs.
method: The authors introduce a 'parallel transport of frames' formalism that generalizes Polyakov's RG to local magnetic anisotropies and dipolar interactions, then apply it to a finite-thickness ultrathin ferromagnetic slab by integrating out short-wavelength spin-wave fluctuations.
result: Integrating out short-wavelength fluctuations generates two emergent local anisotropy terms absent from the microscopic dipolar Hamiltonian; including them yields the experimentally and numerically observed topology of the spin reorientation transition line.
conclusion: The generalized RG framework provides a correct effective description of the spin reorientation transition in ultrathin ferromagnetic slabs, demonstrating the importance of fluctuation-generated anisotropies.

title: The Weak Type $(1,1)$ Estimate Of Dirichlet Means For Unbounded Noncommutative Vilenkin Systems
authors: Tiantian Zhao Guixiang Hong
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30779v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be the hyperfinite [MATH] factor. Considering the partial sum operators [MATH] of the noncommutative Vilenkin-Fourier series associated with an arbitrary admissible Vilenkin group, we prove that there exists a universal constant [MATH] such that \sup_{n\geq1}\|_n(f)\|_{L_{1,\infty}()} \leq c\|f\|_{L_1()},\quad f \in L_1(), and, for every [MATH], $[MATH][MATH](1,1)[MATH]{p-1}$.
tldr: The paper proves a weak type (1,1) estimate for Dirichlet means of noncommutative Vilenkin-Fourier series on the hyperfinite factor.
motivation: Noncommutative harmonic analysis seeks analogues of classical Fourier analysis results in the setting of operator algebras, and Vilenkin systems provide a natural noncommutative generalization of Walsh-Fourier series.
method: The authors analyze partial sum operators associated with arbitrary admissible Vilenkin groups acting on the hyperfinite factor and establish weak type (1,1) and strong type (p,p) bounds.
result: They show that the maximal partial sum operator is bounded from L1 to L1,infinity with a universal constant, and also obtain Lp bounds for p > 1.
conclusion: These results extend classical Dirichlet mean estimates to the noncommutative Vilenkin setting, contributing to noncommutative harmonic analysis but not directly to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Attosecond Topological Interference Beyond Floquet-Volkov Paths
authors: J. D. Lee Hyosub Park
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30282v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Combining attosecond science with semiconductor physics provides a promising interdisciplinary platform for the attosecond control of semiconducting properties. In each field, the reconstruction of attosecond beating by interference of two-photon transitions (RABBIT) and the time-resolved and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (tr-ARPES) have been central experimental techniques for probing microscopic dynamics of electrons. However, the integration of the two techniques, bridging the two fields, has been missing so far although they have many technical similarities. Here, we develop a theoretical framework that integrates the two techniques based on the second-order time-dependent perturbation theory. Within this framework, we investigate the RABBIT spectroscopy in semiconductors focusing on the recent hallmark of tr-ARPES, namely quantum path interference between Floquet and Volkov states. Moreover, we theoretically identify a novel quantum path incorporating the virtual excitation, which substantially interferes with the Floquet and Volkov states in both the RABBIT spectroscopy and tr-ARPES of semiconductors. Importantly, we find that such virtual excitation channel induces an attosecond topological interference with the Floquet-Volkov paths, encoding topological quantities such as the local Berry curvature into the time shift of RABBIT sidebands, which is directly related to the photoelectron emission delay. Our findings establish a theoretical framework connecting attosecond spectroscopy to tr-ARPES, paving the way for future applications of attosecond science in semiconductors.
tldr: The paper develops a theoretical framework integrating RABBIT and tr-ARPES to study attosecond topological interference in semiconductors, identifying a virtual excitation channel that encodes Berry curvature into sideband time shifts.
motivation: Combining attosecond spectroscopy with semiconductor physics could enable attosecond control of material properties, but a unified framework bridging RABBIT and tr-ARPES has been missing.
method: Second-order time-dependent perturbation theory is used to model RABBIT spectroscopy in semiconductors, focusing on quantum path interference between Floquet, Volkov, and a newly identified virtual excitation channel.
result: The virtual excitation channel substantially interferes with Floquet-Volkov paths, producing an attosecond topological interference that encodes local Berry curvature into the time shift of RABBIT sidebands.
conclusion: The work establishes a theoretical connection between attosecond spectroscopy and tr-ARPES, suggesting future applications in semiconductor attosecond science.

title: Skyrmion Topology Of Scalar Waves In Real And Momentum Space
authors: Nai H. Kwong, Ewan M. Wright, Jan Wingenbach, Roman Lebs, Harald Giessen, Stefan Schumacher, Rolf Binder
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30512v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generalizations of magnetic skyrmions to the context of other areas of physics, such as plasmonics, optics (including microcavity polaritons) and even water waves have become an important research topic. However, the generalization of the skyrmion number in such systems is still the subject of active research. While magnetic skyrmions textures are inherently formed by vectors (magnetic spin vectors), recent developments in other areas of physics have generalized the concept of skyrmions and skyrmionic patterns to the case in which scalar fields are used to define 3-component pseudo-spin vectors. This gives rise to a wide variety of skyrmion-like textures, depending on the detailed functional forms of the scalar fields. For example, steady-state outgoing waves in driven-dissipative polariton systems fail to have a well-defined global skyrmion number in real (configuration) space but can have one in momentum space. We classify the skyrmion integral for various scalar fields with different asymptotic behaviors in real space as well as momentum space, and in both cases give conditions for the skyrmion number not to exist, or be integer, half-integer or non-integer. Examples of physical systems to which our analysis can be applied include polariton condensates, water waves and gain-guided lasers.
tldr: The paper classifies the skyrmion number for scalar wave fields in real and momentum space, giving conditions for it to be integer, half-integer, non-integer, or undefined.
motivation: Skyrmion concepts have been generalized to scalar fields in optics, polaritonics, and water waves, but the definition of skyrmion number in such systems remains unsettled.
method: Analyzes the skyrmion integral for various scalar fields with different asymptotic behaviors in real and momentum space, deriving conditions for the topological charge to exist and take specific values.
result: Shows that scalar-wave skyrmion numbers can be integer, half-integer, non-integer, or fail to exist depending on asymptotic behavior and whether real or momentum space is used.
conclusion: Provides a general framework applicable to polariton condensates, water waves, and gain-guided lasers, but it does not address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum platforms.

title: The para--Krawtchouk Oscillator And Its Continuum Limit
authors: St\'ephane Z. Beaulac, Nicolas Cramp\'e, Quentin Labriet, Lucia Morey, Marlon Josue Rivera Valladares, Luc Vinet
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30619v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The para--Krawtchouk polynomials define, through their recurrence relation, a finite oscillator model that carries out fractional revival. We determine the continuum limit of this Hamiltonian, both from its recurrence relation and directly on the polynomials. The limit is the singular (isotonic) oscillator [MATH]: the deformation parameter [MATH] survives as a central impurity of the couplings, decaying as the inverse square of the distance --- the marginal rate, which the continuum scaling turns into a finite [MATH] term. Using the decomposition of the para--Krawtchouk polynomials into two Hahn families, we prove the confluence, for every degree, of the eigenvectors on the two sublattices to generalized Hermite functions. The bispectral pair of the discrete model, which generates the Hahn algebra, becomes in the limit a pair of generators of [MATH], the dynamical algebra of the singular oscillator.
tldr: The paper studies the continuum limit of a finite oscillator defined by para-Krawtchouk polynomials, showing it converges to the singular (isotonic) oscillator and relating their algebraic structures.
motivation: Para-Krawtchouk polynomials define discrete finite oscillator models with fractional revival, and understanding their continuum limit connects them to well-known singular oscillator systems.
method: The authors analyze the recurrence relation and decompose the para-Krawtchouk polynomials into two Hahn families to prove the confluence of eigenvectors on two sublattices to generalized Hermite functions.
result: The continuum limit yields the singular (isotonic) oscillator, where the deformation parameter survives as a central impurity decaying as the inverse square of distance, and the bispectral pair generating the Hahn algebra becomes generators of a dynamical algebra.
conclusion: This work establishes a rigorous algebraic and analytic link between discrete para-Krawtchouk oscillator models and the singular oscillator, extending the understanding of their spectral and algebraic properties.

title: The Supersymmetric Scarf I Hamiltonian With Reflections And Its Discrete para-Bannai--Ito Version
authors: St\'ephane Z. Beaulac, Nicolas Cramp\'e, Quentin Labriet, Lucia Morey, Marlon Josue Rivera Valladares, Luc Vinet
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30636v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The para-Bannai--Ito polynomials are orthogonal on a Bannai--Ito bi-lattice that is --- it extends on both sides of a central value [MATH] --- and depend, besides the two grid parameters, on an isospectral deformation parameter. Their Jacobi matrix [MATH] is invariant under the reversal of the sites at one value of that parameter only, the persymmetric point, and we determine its continuum limit there. Because the grid is two-sided, the natural object is the shifted operator [MATH], and the limit is taken about the centre of the band: [MATH] contracts to a first--order Dunkl operator, a supercharge, and [MATH] to the generalized P\"oschl--Teller (Scarf I) Hamiltonian, with little [MATH] Jacobi eigenfunctions --- supersymmetric quantum mechanics with reflections, the reflection entering the square root of the Hamiltonian. The second grid parameter adds a reflection term to the Hamiltonian itself, and the bi-lattice is, up to a shift, the spectrum of the limiting supercharge. The convergence of the eigenvectors is proved directly on the polynomials. On this grid the persymmetric model transfers states perfectly, under an arithmetic condition on the parameters, but never revives fractionally, revival being the work of the deformation; both properties pass to the limit. These results are for an even number of sites; for an odd number of sites the limit is instead the matrix supersymmetric pair of P\"oschl--Teller Hamiltonians, with the reflection in the Hamiltonian as a Dunkl potential. The bispectral pair of the discrete model goes over to the Dunkl realization of the anticommutator algebra of the little [MATH] Jacobi polynomials.
tldr: The paper analyzes the continuum limit of discrete para-Bannai-Ito polynomials, connecting them to a supersymmetric Scarf I Hamiltonian with reflections and exploring perfect state transfer.
motivation: To understand the algebraic structure of para-Bannai-Ito polynomials and their relationship to supersymmetric quantum mechanics with reflections.
method: The Jacobi matrix is studied in the continuum limit around the band center, yielding a first-order Dunkl operator and a generalized Pöschl-Teller Hamiltonian; convergence of eigenvectors is proved directly.
result: The limit produces a supersymmetric Scarf I Hamiltonian with reflection in the square root, and the bi-lattice becomes the spectrum of the limiting supercharge; perfect state transfer and absence of fractional revival pass to the limit.
conclusion: The discrete model's bispectral pair corresponds to the Dunkl realization of the anticommutator algebra of little Jacobi polynomials, linking discrete orthogonal polynomials to continuous SUSY QM.

title: Laser Induced Broad Band White Emission From Transparent Cr4+:YAG Ceramics: Origin Of Broadband Emission
authors: W. Strek M. Chaika
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30907v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Laser-induced white (light) emission was observed from transparent Cr:YAG ceramics irradiated with a focused continuous wave beam of light from an infrared laser diode. The laser-induced white emission is detected only on the surface of the sample and is not observed in volume. It is found that the intensity of the emission increases exponentially with the laser power density above the threshold. The impact of broadband emission on the power of the transmitted laser beam through the sample was measured. The disappearance of broadband emission due to displacement of the laser beam or an increase in ambient pressure leads to a decrease in the power of transmitted laser beam. Origins of the laser-induced white light emission along with its characteristic features are discussed in terms of multiphoton absorption, intervalence charge transfer and ionic space charge models.
tldr: Laser-induced broadband white emission is observed from the surface of transparent Cr4+:YAG ceramics under focused continuous-wave infrared laser irradiation, with possible origins discussed via multiphoton absorption, intervalence charge transfer, and ionic space charge models.
motivation: The study aims to understand the origin and characteristics of laser-induced white light emission in transparent Cr:YAG ceramics, a phenomenon relevant to developing broadband light sources and clarifying laser-matter interactions in doped dielectric materials.
method: Transparent Cr4+:YAG ceramic samples are irradiated with a focused continuous-wave infrared laser diode; the emitted white light is measured as a function of laser power density, beam position, and ambient pressure, while transmitted laser power is also monitored.
result: The white emission appears only on the sample surface, not in the volume, and grows exponentially with laser power above a threshold; displacing the beam or increasing ambient pressure extinguishes the emission and reduces transmitted laser power.
conclusion: The observations suggest that the broadband emission originates from multiphoton absorption, intervalence charge transfer, and ionic space charge effects, though a definitive microscopic mechanism remains to be established.

title: Reachability Does Not Imply Searchability In Expanding Networks
authors: Antonio Scala
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31042v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Routing and search respond in opposite ways to rapid network expansion. Short graph distances make a known destination easy to reach, while the neighborhood accessible within a few hops can be vastly larger than any finite inspection budget. We show that this tension imposes an algorithm-independent constraint on sparse search. If [MATH] relevant nodes are placed without structural information among [MATH] nodes and at most [MATH] nodes can be inspected, any target-blind exploration protocol has success probability at most [MATH], irrespective of correlations between successive inspections, of revisits, and of any structural preference the exploration rule may have. Geometry determines when this constraint becomes relevant: a target becomes accessible with order-one probability when the graph-distance ball volume satisfies [MATH]. At this scale, any inspection mechanism achieving a fixed success probability [MATH] must enrich the probability of inspecting relevant nodes by at least order [MATH] relative to the neutral target density. For uniformly searched candidate sets, this entails a vanishing visible fraction of the accessible region. Thus rapidly expanding networks can make rare targets geometrically close while target-blind search remains ineffective. Numerical results on Krioukov hyperbolic random graphs and two-dimensional lattices show that this separation can arise within only a few hops in the rapidly expanding case, while the lattice accessibility radius grows algebraically.
tldr: The paper proves that in rapidly expanding sparse networks, short graph distances do not imply efficient target-blind search, due to an algorithm-independent constraint on inspection-based exploration.
motivation: Routing and search behave oppositely under network expansion: known destinations can be reached via short paths, but unknown targets become hard to find when the accessible neighborhood vastly exceeds any finite inspection budget.
method: The authors derive a universal upper bound on the success probability of any target-blind exploration protocol, then analyze when this bound becomes relevant in terms of graph-distance ball volume. They validate predictions numerically on Krioukov hyperbolic random graphs and two-dimensional lattices.
result: The success probability is bounded independently of correlations, revisits, or structural preferences. In expanding networks, order-one accessibility requires the inspection mechanism to enrich relevant-node visitation probability at least proportionally to the inverse target density, leading to a vanishing visible fraction of the accessible region.
conclusion: Rapidly expanding networks can make rare targets geometrically close while still rendering target-blind search ineffective, with the separation emerging within a few hops for hyperbolic graphs but only algebraically for lattices.

title: Best Constants In Noncommutative Burkholder Inequalities
authors: Yong Jiao, Adam Osekowski, Lian Wu, Yahui Zuo
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30600v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The paper contains the study of noncommutative Burkholder inequalities. We prove that the constant involved is of order [MATH] when [MATH], which is known to be optimal even in the commutative setting. This answers an open problem raised by Randrianantoanina in 2007, and by Junge and Xu in 2008.
tldr: The paper determines the optimal constant in noncommutative Burkholder inequalities, resolving open problems from 2007/2008.
motivation: Noncommutative Burkholder inequalities are central in noncommutative martingale theory, but the best constant for the general case remained unknown.
method: The authors prove sharp estimates for martingale transforms in noncommutative Lp spaces, showing the constant is of order sqrt(p) and optimal even in the commutative setting.
result: They establish the optimal order of the constant in noncommutative Burkholder inequalities, answering questions by Randrianantoanina and by Junge and Xu.
conclusion: The work advances the mathematical theory of noncommutative martingale inequalities, but it lies outside the quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid systems research directions.

title: A Class Of Shift-Invariant Permutations And Their Algebraic Structure
authors: Cheng Lyu, Dabin Zheng, Mu Yuan, Lei Hu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31174v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Shift-invariant permutations of [MATH] are attractive in symmetric cryptography because of their regularity and implementation efficiency. Constructing such permutations with an explicit algebraic structure remains a challenging problem. In this paper, we study a family of shift-invariant transformations of [MATH] generated by a recursively defined sequence of mappings [MATH] associated with landscapes. First, we prove that, under an explicit dimension condition on [MATH] and the support of the landscape, the sequence [MATH] has the polynomial composition property if and only if the corresponding landscape with nonzero special index is quasi-conserved on [MATH]. Then, we determine the eventual zero or periodic behavior of [MATH], including the first zero or periodic index and the least eventual period, and establish linear independence up to the first relation. When the polynomial composition property holds, we establish an explicit isomorphism between the group of permutation elements in the monoid generated by these mappings and the unit group of a quotient ring [MATH], where [MATH] is a monomial or a binomial determined by the landscape. This framework reduces the permutation property, compositional inverse, order, and iterates of these mappings to polynomial computations. Finally, we apply the results to mappings represented by binomials and trinomials in the quotient ring, obtaining explicit criteria and formulas. We tabulate more than one hundred representative constructions of shift-invariant permutations, recovering and unifying several previously studied families.
tldr: This paper studies a family of shift-invariant permutations over finite sets using recursively defined mappings and landscape functions, with applications to symmetric cryptography.
motivation: Shift-invariant permutations are attractive in symmetric cryptography due to their regularity and implementation efficiency, but constructing them with explicit algebraic structure remains challenging.
method: The authors analyze recursively defined mapping sequences associated with landscapes, proving conditions for the polynomial composition property based on quasi-conserved landscapes and establishing an isomorphism between a monoid's permutation group and the unit group of a quotient ring.
result: They determine eventual zero or periodic behavior, linear independence, and reduce permutation properties, compositional inverses, orders, and iterates to polynomial computations, applying the framework to binomial and trinomial mappings and tabulating over one hundred constructions.
conclusion: The framework unifies and recovers several previously studied families of shift-invariant permutations, providing explicit criteria and formulas for cryptographic constructions.

title: Failure Of The P\'olya-Szeg\H{o} Inequality For The Fractional Gradient
authors: Giorgio Stefani
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31233v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that the P\'olya-Szeg inequality for the [MATH] norm of the Riesz fractional [MATH]-gradient fails for every [MATH] and [MATH], thus providing a negative answer to a question posed by Nguyen and Squassina in 2017.
tldr: The paper disproves the Pólya-Szegő inequality for the Riesz fractional gradient for all relevant parameter ranges.
motivation: A question posed by Nguyen and Squassina in 2017 asked whether the Pólya-Szegő inequality extends to the fractional gradient setting.
method: The author constructs counterexamples and proves that the inequality fails for every admissible fractional order and dimension.
result: The Pólya-Szegő inequality for the L^p norm of the Riesz fractional gradient is shown to fail universally.
conclusion: This resolves the open question negatively and indicates that classical symmetrization results do not carry over to fractional nonlocal operators.

title: Linear Certificates For Membership Comparability, Quadratic Barriers For Selectors
authors: Sebastian Ben Daniel
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31053v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Selectors and comparators supply only partial information about membership: a selector names a member of any pair that meets the language, while a binary membership comparator merely excludes one of the four membership vectors of a pair. We ask how much nonuniform advice turns such information into exact recognition. Our main result extends the optimal nondeterministic advice bound for P-selective sets to every binary membership-comparable language: [MATH], with common fixed advice and certificates of at most [MATH] bits. The class is strictly larger; some 2-mc sets are not truth-table reducible to any P-selective set. The proof replaces the tournament king by an independent two-step cover of true signed literals, together with a short-forcing-or-exact-majority dichotomy, and it relativizes. Via an advice-preserving isolation transfer, a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for promise Unique-Circuit-SAT gives [MATH]. For selectors we determine tight orders of ordinary advice: [MATH] for errorless average-case computation and [MATH] for worst-case bounded-error computation, the latter independent of the interpreter's coin bound. One oracle realizes both orders on a single language and separates ordinary from coin-dependent advice. The quadratic and linear lower bounds hold for tournament-query procedures and relativized languages, not unconditionally for unrelativized P-selective sets.
tldr: This paper studies how nonuniform advice and certificates enable exact recognition from partial membership information given by selectors and comparators, establishing linear certificates and quadratic barriers in computational complexity.
motivation: Selectors and membership comparators provide only partial information about language membership, and the paper asks how much nonuniform advice is needed to convert such partial information into exact recognition.
method: The authors use combinatorial covering arguments for true signed literals, a short-forcing-or-exact-majority dichotomy, and an advice-preserving isolation transfer to prove upper bounds and lower bounds for binary membership-comparable languages and selectors.
result: The main results extend optimal nondeterministic advice bounds to binary membership-comparable languages, show quadratic barriers for selector-based computation, and separate ordinary from coin-dependent advice using an oracle.
conclusion: The findings clarify the complexity of exact recognition from partial membership information, but they lie in classical computational complexity and are not directly connected to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: BenX: Resource-Sharing Permutations For Computational Integrity
authors: Luca Campa, Thomas de Cnudde, Al Kindi, Arnab Roy, Fabian Schmid, Markus Schofnegger, Stefano Trevisani
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cryptographic hash functions over integers modulo a prime play a decisive role in the efficiency and security of proof systems for computational integrity. Early designs focused on compact arithmetic circuits and efficient software execution, primarily targeting general-purpose CPUs rather than hardware accelerators. This work focuses on enabling efficient resource sharing and hardware acceleration alongside efficient software execution. We propose BenX, a permutation-based hash function designed for hardware acceleration, fast CPU execution, and low circuit complexity in proof systems. To construct the underlying permutation, we turn the Benes network into an invertible function over [MATH] using a Dickson polynomial. Its structure yields a permutation particularly suited to hardware resource sharing and acceleration. Fully pipelined on FPGA, BenX matches the throughput of Poseidon2, with 1.36x and 2.15x lower latency for Goldilocks and BabyBear, respectively. Although larger as a standalone core, it makes more effective use of shared hardware: in our dual-mode architecture, where the NTT and hash share field multipliers, BenX keeps 100% of them busy, compared with 6.25-20.3% for the partial rounds of Poseidon and Poseidon2. In software, BenX outperforms Poseidon in all tested 31- and 64-bit configurations, but is slower than Poseidon2, except for the 16-element BabyBear instance. In zero-knowledge proofs, BenX proves Goldilocks permutations 6-10x faster than Monolith. Its compact arithmetization uses about 36% fewer trace cells than Poseidon and Poseidon2 over BabyBear, while its fast variant requires 1.3-2.6x the prover time of Poseidon2.
tldr: BenX is a permutation-based cryptographic hash function designed for hardware acceleration and low circuit complexity in proof systems for computational integrity.
motivation: Existing hash functions for proof systems target CPUs rather than hardware accelerators, limiting resource sharing and efficiency in FPGA implementations.
method: The authors construct an invertible permutation over a prime field using a Benes network and Dickson polynomial, enabling efficient resource sharing between NTT and hash operations.
result: BenX matches Poseidon2 throughput with lower latency, achieves high field multiplier utilization in dual-mode architecture, outperforms Poseidon in software, and proves Goldilocks permutations 6-10x faster than Monolith in zero-knowledge proofs.
conclusion: BenX demonstrates that permutation-based hash functions can be optimized for both hardware and software in proof systems, offering improved resource sharing despite larger core size.

title: Revisiting Certified Defense With Differential Privacy On Vision Transformers
authors: Jun Yan, Weiquan Huang, Qixian Zhang, Yan Bai, Shutai Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31310v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Certified defenses that incorporate differential privacy have proven effective on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), furnishing rigorous robustness guarantees against norm-bounded adversaries. However, the certified robustness behavior of Pixel Differential Privacy (PixelDP) remains largely unexplored with the self-attention architecture now dominating the deep-learning landscape. Given that the Transformer has a profound impact on our daily applications from the digital world to the physical world, it is crucial to study certified robustness through differential-privacy-style stability. To fill this research gap, we revisit this construction in Vision Transformers and identify a failure mode that is largely hidden in the convolutional setting. When noise is injected after the patch embedding, the Laplace mechanism with the inherited grouped [MATH] sensitivity bound collapses to chance-level accuracy across noise scales, whereas the Gaussian mechanism remains trainable. This contrast isolates the source of failure: not the injected noise itself, but the geometry of the sensitivity constraint. We show that the attenuation induced by the inherited [MATH] projection increases with layer width and kernel size according to a random-matrix scale [MATH]. Replacing the [MATH]-type constraint with a spectral-norm constraint eliminates the collapse across datasets and architectures, but creates a fundamental obstacle: the repaired models no longer satisfy the sensitivity condition required by the standard Laplace certificate. We resolve this mismatch by deriving a dimension-free [MATH]-privacy guarantee for the Laplace mechanism under [MATH] sensitivity through concentration of the privacy loss.
tldr: The paper studies certified robustness via differential privacy in Vision Transformers, identifying a failure mode of PixelDP with Laplace noise after patch embedding and proposing a spectral-norm constraint plus a dimension-free privacy guarantee.
motivation: Certified defenses with differential privacy have been successful for CNNs but remain unexplored for Vision Transformers, which now dominate deep learning. The authors aim to fill this gap by revisiting PixelDP in the self-attention architecture.
method: They analyze PixelDP in Vision Transformers, compare Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms under grouped L2 sensitivity, identify attenuation scaling with layer width and kernel size, replace the L2-type constraint with a spectral-norm constraint, and derive a dimension-free Rényi privacy guarantee for the Laplace mechanism under L1 sensitivity.
result: The inherited L2 projection causes Laplace-mechanism accuracy to collapse to chance level across noise scales, while the Gaussian mechanism remains trainable; the spectral-norm repair eliminates collapse but violates the standard Laplace certificate, which is resolved by the new dimension-free guarantee.
conclusion: The failure mode originates from sensitivity geometry rather than injected noise, and the proposed spectral-norm constraint with a new Laplace privacy bound offers a path toward certified robustness for Vision Transformers.

title: $u(1)$ Gauge-Equivariant Representation Learning Of Bloch States
authors: Chengyan Zhang, Xian Xu, Bowen Hou, Diana Y. Qiu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30845v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Representation learning, or featurization, of mean-field Bloch states provides an important route for incorporating electronic information into machine-learning models of first-principles condensed-phase systems. A challenge in representing Bloch states is the gauge redundancy of each state. In this work, we propose to address this issue by explicitly incorporating gauge equivariance in the machine-learning framework. We develop a [MATH]-equivariant autoencoder that compresses the plane-wave-basis Bloch states obtained from density functional theory into a low-dimensional latent representation. We achieve an average overlap of 0.970 between original wavefunctions and the reconstructions from a 64-dimensional latent space using a dataset of two-dimensional insulators. We further show that [MATH] equivariance endows the latent space with physically meaningful structures, including smoothness and topological information. Finally, we present a proof-of-principle application in which the latent representations are used to predict the off-diagonal elements of the [MATH] self energy matrix, and demonstrate the importance of enforcing gauge equivariance in the prediction.
tldr: A U(1)-gauge-equivariant autoencoder compresses DFT Bloch states into low-dimensional latent representations and predicts self-energy matrix elements.
motivation: Representation learning for mean-field Bloch states is hindered by gauge redundancy, and enforcing gauge equivariance may yield physically meaningful latent spaces.
method: The authors develop a U(1)-equivariant autoencoder for plane-wave-basis Bloch states from DFT, compressing them to a 64-dimensional latent space and applying the latents to predict off-diagonal self-energy matrix elements.
result: They achieve an average wavefunction overlap of 0.970 on 2D insulators, find that equivariance endows the latent space with smoothness and topological information, and show improved self-energy prediction when enforcing gauge equivariance.
conclusion: Gauge-equivariant representation learning offers a promising route to incorporating electronic-structure information into machine-learning models of condensed-phase systems.

title: A Kinetic Theory Approach To Ordered Fluids: Direct Simulation Monte Carlo Methods
authors: Jos\'e A. Carrillo, Patrick E. Farrell, Andrea Medaglia, Umberto Zerbinati
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31072v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method for the kinetic theory of ordered fluids recently introduced by the authors. The microscopic constituents of these fluids carry an order parameter belonging to a manifold. The method applies Strang splitting to couple a Monte Carlo treatment of the binary collisions with a symplectic integration of the mean-field Vlasov transport on the order-parameter manifold. We use the Nanbu-Babovsky approach for Maxwellian collision kernels, and Bird's acceptance-rejection method for general ones. The mean-field Vlasov force is reconstructed from the particle ensemble at each time step. We also include a Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook (BGK) / Andersen thermostat to control the system temperature. We formulate the method for a generic order-parameter manifold, and specialize it to two-dimensional calamitic (rod-like) molecules. Numerical tests validate the method. We confirm the relaxation to the Maxwellian distribution predicted by the H-theorem, and simulate the mean-field alignment driven by quadratic, Kuramoto, and Onsager interaction potentials. With the Onsager potential we successfully capture the isotropic-nematic phase transition at the correct critical temperature.
tldr: The paper develops a direct simulation Monte Carlo method for kinetic theory of ordered fluids with an order-parameter manifold, validated on rod-like molecules and the isotropic-nematic phase transition.
motivation: Ordered fluids whose microscopic constituents carry an order parameter require kinetic-theory simulation methods beyond standard particle-based approaches.
method: A Strang splitting couples Monte Carlo binary collisions (Nanbu-Babovsky and Bird acceptance-rejection) with symplectic integration of mean-field Vlasov transport on the order-parameter manifold, plus a BGK/Andersen thermostat.
result: Numerical tests confirm relaxation to the Maxwellian distribution predicted by the H-theorem and reproduce mean-field alignment for quadratic, Kuramoto, and Onsager potentials, including the isotropic-nematic transition at the correct critical temperature.
conclusion: The DSMC framework provides a general and validated numerical approach for kinetic simulations of ordered fluids on arbitrary order-parameter manifolds.

title: Quantum Laurent Positivity In Rank Three
authors: Qiyue Tang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30387v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove Laurent positivity for skew-symmetrizable quantum cluster algebras of rank three, with arbitrary integral compatible quantizations and invertible frozen variables. The proof uses mutation-acyclic positivity from a companion manuscript.
tldr: The paper proves Laurent positivity for skew-symmetrizable quantum cluster algebras of rank three.
motivation: Laurent positivity is a fundamental structural property in cluster algebra theory, and the quantum deformation version is less understood.
method: The proof uses mutation-acyclic positivity from a companion manuscript, covering arbitrary integral compatible quantizations and invertible frozen variables.
result: Laurent positivity is established for rank-three skew-symmetrizable quantum cluster algebras.
conclusion: The work advances the mathematical theory of quantum cluster algebras but lies outside the user's listed research directions in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid systems.

title: Scaffold-Constrained Subset Dynamic Programming For Exact Sse Clustering
authors: Max A. Little Yordan P. Raykov
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30477v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exact Euclidean \(K\)-means partitions \(n\) observations into \(K\) unlabelled clusters, but the unrestricted search is generally exponential. We use data-derived geometric graphs to precondition an exact subset dynamic program: as a result only connected vertex subsets are admitted as clusters, while sum-of-squared-errors (SSE) loss is unchanged. A remaining-set recurrence minimises fixed-\(K\) or penalised SSE, with exact factorisation over the connected components of each remaining set. The central question we study is how much computational support can be removed while preserving an unrestricted optimum. Graph inclusion gives monotone coverage and support relations, and a bottleneck threshold identifies the first covering graph in a nested hierarchy. For fixed \(K\) and dimension, under compact ball support and density bounds, retaining \(q=O(\log n)\) nearest neighbours per observation preserves an empirical SSE optimum with probability tending to one, using an \(O(\log n/n)\) fraction of complete-graph edges. Truncated Gaussian mixtures with unequal weights and covariances satisfy these conditions. The rate we provide is a sufficient upper bound rather than a result implying polynomial optimisation complexity. Objective-matched synthetic and full-data comparisons assess coverage, compression, and reference-label agreement. As a secondary application, we illustrate how the proposed scaffold preconditioning can be utilized to improve the efficiency of split-merge proposals that preserve unrestricted mixture posteriors.
tldr: The paper develops scaffold-constrained subset dynamic programming for exact Euclidean K-means/SSE clustering by restricting clusters to connected vertex subsets in data-derived geometric graphs.
motivation: Exact K-means clustering is generally exponential, and the authors aim to reduce computational support while preserving an unrestricted optimum.
method: They use geometric graphs and connected-component factorization to precondition a remaining-set dynamic program, with nearest-neighbour sparsification and a bottleneck threshold in a nested graph hierarchy.
result: Under compact ball support and density bounds, retaining q=O(log n) nearest neighbours preserves an empirical SSE optimum with probability tending to one, using an O(log n/n) fraction of complete-graph edges.
conclusion: The approach provides sufficient conditions for computational compression in exact SSE clustering and can also improve split-merge proposals in mixture posterior sampling.

title: Disjunctive Submodular Functions: Envelopes And Applications To Inventory And 0-1 Quadratic Optimization
authors: Zhongqi Wu, Taotao He, Mohit Tawarmalani
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper considers convex envelopes of disjunctive submodular functions---functions that are lattice family submodular over faces of a hypercube---and constructs the first strongly polynomial algorithm for their separation when there are two facial disjunctions. Submodular functions, whose convex envelopes are characterized by the Lov\'asz extension, have occupied a fundamental role in constructing relaxations for combinatorial and nonlinear optimization problems. However, disjunctive submodular function envelopes have not been explored besides the use of ellipsoid algorithm, which remains practically intractable. Our algorithm is derived in three steps by expressing the disjunctive function as a minimum of two extended submodular functions, introducing a variable lifting technique, and constructing the sublinear envelope in the lifted space. The paper also makes several other contributions. First, we provide a disjunctive formulation for the case where each submodular function admits a linear programming formulation. Second, we derive the closed-form sublinear envelope characterization for intersecting submodular functions, yielding new structural insights into a multi-product inventory sales maximization problem. Third, we fully characterize the convex envelope of a bilinear function defined over a cycle graph in the original variable space. Finally, we show computationally that the cycle inequalities close approximately 60\% of the gap for complete and Hadamard graphs, over 30\% of the gap for complete bipartite graphs, and over 80\% of the gap for sparse graphs such as cactus and Halin graphs.
