Once the cutoff may vary across rounds, even such rules cannot guarantee JR or PSC for groups that agree in only some rounds. For groups that agree in every round, however, knowing only the number of rounds suffices for PJR in polynomial time, and PSC needs no knowledge of the future at all. Under individual cutoffs, no version of JR or PJR can be guaranteed, yet a rule as simple as serial dictatorship achieves PJR up to an additive loss that no rule can improve on, however much it knows. Natural preference restrictions restore exact guarantees. Finally, we show that checking our axioms is often coNP-complete; but perhaps surprisingly, a stronger axiom can be easier to check.
tldr: The paper studies proportional representation axioms for temporal voting with ranked preferences, characterizing which axioms can be guaranteed under different cutoff interpretations and knowledge of the future.
motivation: Prior work on temporal voting has focused on approval ballots, but ranked preferences that may change over time require a generalized notion of proportionality since the appropriate approval cutoff varies across voters and rounds.
method: The authors define hierarchies of proportionality axioms (JR, PJR, EJR, PSC) parameterized by admissible cutoff choices—fixed common, common but varying across rounds, or individual per voter per round—and analyze which can be satisfied under varying degrees of foresight, proving complexity results and additive guarantees.
result: No version of EJR is achievable; with a fixed common cutoff JR, PJR, and PSC are attainable only by clairvoyant rules, while varying cutoffs break JR/PSC guarantees, and under individual cutoffs serial dictatorship achieves optimal additive PJR loss; axiom checking is often coNP-complete.
conclusion: Ranked temporal voting yields a fundamentally different, more constrained proportionality landscape than approval-based voting, with tradeoffs between cutoff flexibility and guaranteed representation.

title: Subjects, Not Authors: The Authorship Hazard In Agentic Dataspaces
authors: Changbin Lee Seungho Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30614v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dataspace connectors decide whether a transfer may occur, not what the transferred value contains, tolerable for contracted applications, not for LLM agents that compose tool calls and spawn sub-agents. Research on agents that generate governance artifacts evaluates output quality; who may authorize an artifact for use falls between that literature and the governance literature, and neither owns it. A published policy is what a dataspace's decision point enforces, so publication is a governance event, and an agent that is both policy subject and policy author writes the norms that bind it. We name this the authorship hazard and state one principle: an agent is a subject of the governance plane, never an author of it. Its authorization channel to publication is closed by construction; its influence channel, drafting what humans approve, is treated as an enforcement problem. On a frozen corpus of agent drafts, publishing without approval reverses 80 authorization decisions, most through drafts that change only a field's sensitivity classification and no policy text; a classifier that reads the policy diff misses every such draft, necessarily. Treating classification as authorship routes them all to review; the registry-held classification this requires is designed and modelled here, not yet implemented in the prototype. At the execution boundary, protected fields reach the model in 105 of 105 cases under prompt-stated duties and in 0 of 105 when the ODRL duty is compiled into an invocation-time tool-call constraint, but where the value is not confined to a named field the compiled condition exposes it in 7 of 7. A centrally provisioned approval pool does not scale to the participant volume that motivates the problem.
tldr: The paper identifies an 'authorship hazard' in agentic dataspaces and argues that LLM agents must be policy subjects rather than policy authors, proposing a registry-held classification and compiled ODRL invocation-time constraints to enforce this.
motivation: LLM agents that draft governance artifacts can effectively author the very policies that bind them, and existing work on agent-generated governance or on dataspaces' transfer-decision connectors does not address who may authorize an artifact for use.
method: The authors analyze a frozen corpus of agent policy drafts, compare publishing with and without human approval, test a policy-diff-reading classifier, and model a registry-held classification scheme plus ODRL duty compilation at the tool-call boundary.
result: Publishing without approval reverses 80 authorization decisions, mostly via drafts changing only a sensitivity classification field that a policy-diff classifier necessarily misses; compiled invocation-time constraints reduce protected-field exposure from 105/105 to 0/105, though non-field-confined values still leak in 7/7 cases.
conclusion: Treating classification as a governance act routes hazardous drafts to review, but the proposed registry is designed and modelled only, and a centrally provisioned approval pool does not scale to realistic participant volumes.

title: A Large-Scale Empirical Study Of Modern Phishing Email Content
authors: Jaehwan Park, Woonghee Lee, Fujiao Ji, Doowon Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Phishing remains one of the most pervasive threats to Internet users, and email remains its predominant delivery channel. Email content is the attack surface of phishing: it is what the victim reads and what automated defenses inspect. Yet the composition of modern phishing content is poorly measured. Prior work has characterized dimensions such as theme, call-to-action (CTA), and impersonation, but not at scale, and their associations and temporal changes remain unclear, owing to small or source-specific corpora, bag-of-words topic models, and a focus on text alone. We present a content-focused measurement study of 2.9M distinct real-world phishing emails collected over 13 months (June 2025 - June 2026) in collaboration with the Anti-Phishing Working Group (APWG). We treat each email as a composite artifact comprising message text and its attachments: 272K images, 143K PDFs, and 57K calendar invitations. Using an LLM pipeline validated against human-annotated samples, we analyze these components along three dimensions (theme, CTA, and impersonation), examine the associations among them, and measure longer-term change against a historical dataset. We find that attackers diversify what they use to deceive but converge on how victims should respond: no theme exceeds 21.3% of emails, while a single CTA, URL navigation, accounts for 73.0%. CTA and impersonation choices are conditioned on theme. Attachments play three roles: images supplement the message text, PDFs substitute for it by carrying the pretext, and calendar invitations reinforce it by replicating interaction endpoints into a persistent medium. Over the longer term, the dominant CTA for invoice-themed phishing shifted from URL navigation to offline communication, rising from 6.7% in 2015 to 46.9% in 2025.
tldr: A large-scale measurement study of 2.9M real-world phishing emails using an LLM annotation pipeline to characterize theme, call-to-action, and impersonation across text and attachments.
motivation: Email content is the primary attack surface of phishing, yet the composition of modern phishing content is poorly measured at scale due to small, source-specific corpora and shallow bag-of-words topic models focused on text alone.
method: The authors analyze 2.9M distinct phishing emails collected over 13 months with the APWG, treating each email as a composite of message text plus attachments (272K images, 143K PDFs, 57K calendar invites), and use a human-validated LLM pipeline to annotate theme, CTA, and impersonation, with a historical comparison for temporal change.
result: Attackers diversify deception themes (no theme exceeds 21.3%) but converge on response mechanics (URL navigation CTA = 73.0%); CTA and impersonation depend on theme, and attachments serve supplementary, substitutive, or reinforcing roles. Invoice-themed phishing shifted from URL navigation (6.7% in 2015) to offline communication (46.9% in 2025).
conclusion: Modern phishing content shows strategic diversity in pretexts with strong convergence in call-to-action, and temporal drift toward offline communication channels, highlighting the value of large-scale, multimodal content measurement for defense.

title: From Bilateral Trade To Matching Markets: Sharp Gains From Trade
authors: Zhengyang Liu, Ying Qin, Zihe Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30702v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study gains from trade in matching markets with independent private values and costs, Bayesian incentive compatibility, interim individual rationality, and no expected budget deficit. A second-best guarantee for finite bilateral trade extends without loss to matching markets with independent Borel priors, arbitrary downward-closed feasibility, and finite expected first-best gains. For bounded buyers with monotone hazard rates and arbitrary bounded sellers, we determine the exact worst-case ratio of second-best to first-best gains, approximately [MATH]. For binary buyers and sellers with at most [MATH] types, we determine the exact ratio for every [MATH], including [MATH] when [MATH] and a limit of [MATH] as [MATH] grows. Both families of bounds are tight already in bilateral trade.
tldr: The paper extends sharp second-best-to-first-best gains-from-trade bounds from bilateral trade to matching markets with independent private values and general downward-closed feasibility constraints.
motivation: Bilateral trade gives a canonical benchmark for how much welfare is lost under Bayesian incentive compatibility, individual rationality, and budget balance, but it was unclear whether those guarantees and their tight constants carry over to multi-agent matching settings.
method: The authors generalize the second-best guarantee to matching markets with independent Borel priors and arbitrary downward-closed feasibility, then derive exact worst-case ratios analytically for bounded buyers with monotone hazard rates and for binary buyer/seller type families.
result: A second-best guarantee for finite bilateral trade extends losslessly to matching markets, exact worst-case ratios are obtained (approximately 0.998 and binary-type values such as 0.9999 with a limit of 1), and all bounds are tight already in bilateral trade.
conclusion: Sharp gains-from-trade limits are shown to be fundamentally a bilateral phenomenon, giving exact mechanism-design benchmarks for matching markets under standard Bayesian constraints.

title: XPhysICS: Cross-Physical-Domain Threat Grounding For Industrial Control Systems Security
authors: Sangshin Park, Jainta Paul, Lawrence Ponce, Md Raihan Ahmed, Mu Zhang, Luis Garcia
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30805v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Industrial control system (ICS) threats documented for one plant can express cyber-physical effects relevant to another, but semantic similarity alone does not establish whether those effects are structurally admissible or evaluable on a target. We present XPhysICS, a provenance-aware, target-conditioned method that separates analyst-guided source abstraction from deterministic grounding into target-specific validation slices. Given a fixed source abstraction, vocabulary and schema, and machine-validated target contract, XPhysICS evaluates candidate mappings using five eligibility criteria: role compatibility, implemented type compatibility, stage coherence, slice viability, and rule-surface applicability. Grounding acceptance, slice adequacy, dynamic realizability, consumer applicability, and consumer outcome remain distinct evidence layers. We evaluate 83 structured source-threat abstractions across water treatment, water distribution, hydro/water-energy, and chemical-process targets. Controlled target-side studies of SWaT-to-water-treatment and WADI-to-water-distribution groundings produce clean, nominal-confounded, and near-threshold consumer outcomes; nine Hydro/GRFICS cases extend bounded validation-slice execution. We also evaluate bounded predictive, state-aware, and phase-aware consumer lanes, the unmodified upstream GeCo implementation, and a paper-derived reproduction of a physics-guided search method over three frozen groundings. Results show that cross-domain ICS threat reuse requires traceable source semantics, explicit target-conditioned grounding criteria, and careful separation of subsequent target-side evidence.
tldr: XPhysICS is a provenance-aware, target-conditioned framework for grounding industrial control system (ICS) threat abstractions across physical domains so that documented cyber-physical effects from one plant can be validated for structural admissibility on another.
motivation: ICS threat intelligence from one facility may carry cyber-physical effects relevant to another, but semantic similarity alone cannot establish whether those effects are structurally admissible or evaluable on a specific target system.
method: The approach separates analyst-guided source abstraction from deterministic grounding into target-specific validation slices, evaluating candidate mappings via five eligibility criteria (role compatibility, implemented type compatibility, stage coherence, slice viability, rule-surface applicability) while keeping grounding acceptance, slice adequacy, dynamic realizability, and consumer evidence layers distinct.
result: Evaluated on 83 structured source-threat abstractions across water treatment, distribution, hydro/water-energy, and chemical-process targets, including SWaT-to-water-treatment and WADI-to-water-distribution studies, nine Hydro/GRFICS cases, and comparisons against an unmodified GeCo implementation and a physics-guided search baseline.
conclusion: Cross-domain ICS threat reuse demands traceable source semantics, explicit target-conditioned grounding criteria, and careful separation of downstream target-side evidence layers.

title: MetaPermit: Scalable And Auditable Access Control For Ai Agents Via LLM-Inferred Meta-Attributes
authors: Hanzhang Ma, Ali Hariri, Tianxiang Shen, Bohua Zou, Qianjun Zheng, Ji Wang, Li Yi, Ning Jia, Yutao Liu, Haibo Chen, Lin Wang, Debayan Roy
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31039v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rise of autonomous AI agents equipped with tools has introduced significant security risks, ranging from unintended tool misuse to adversarial manipulation through Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) attacks. In practice, deployed agent systems such as OpenAI Codex and Claude Code protect tool invocations through a combination of coarse-grained permission rules and LLM-based judgments about individual proposed actions. Both components, however, have important limitations: static policies must anticipate possible user intents and therefore do not scale to open-ended tasks, while LLM-driven authorization supports dynamic decisions but produces inconsistent outcomes and remains vulnerable to targeted IPI attacks. To provide scalable and more consistent authorization, we propose MetaPermit, a policy-based tool access-control framework that decouples semantic inference from security enforcement. By analyzing agent-user interactions, we derive a compact, task-independent set of meta-attributes that capture the relationships among the user's intent, the execution context, and the proposed tool call. These meta-attributes allow MetaPermit to authorize tool use without enumerating user intents. At runtime, an LLM infers the meta-attribute values for each proposed tool call, while a fixed policy evaluates these values to allow or deny the call, making each decision auditable through the inferred values and the applied policy rule. We evaluate MetaPermit on the AgentDojo and AgentDyn benchmarks, across seven task suites and five attack methods, using two widely deployed open-weight LLMs. The results show that MetaPermit produces 31% more consistent authorization decisions than LLM-driven authorization and outperforms the state-of-the-art defenses CaMeL and IPIGuard in both task completion, with improvements of up to 109%, and robustness to IPI attacks, with no malicious tool calls executed.
tldr: MetaPermit is a policy-based tool access-control framework for autonomous AI agents that decouples LLM-based semantic inference of task-independent meta-attributes from fixed, auditable security enforcement policies.
motivation: Deployed LLM agent systems rely on coarse-grained static permission rules that fail to scale to open-ended tasks, or on LLM-driven authorization that yields inconsistent decisions and remains vulnerable to indirect prompt injection attacks.
method: The authors derive a compact, task-independent set of meta-attributes relating user intent, execution context, and the proposed tool call; at runtime an LLM infers meta-attribute values that a fixed policy evaluates to allow or deny each tool invocation, making decisions auditable.
result: Evaluated on AgentDojo and AgentDyn across seven task suites, five attack methods, and two open-weight LLMs, MetaPermit produced 31% more consistent authorization decisions than LLM-driven authorization and improved task completion by up to 109% over CaMeL and IPIGuard while preventing all malicious tool calls.
conclusion: MetaPermit offers a scalable, consistent, and auditable approach to tool-access control for AI agents, improving both utility and robustness against indirect prompt injection compared to state-of-the-art defenses.

title: Sadra: Sound Capability-based Access Control System For Resource-Disaggregated Architectures
authors: Hamed Rasifard, Amir Farahani Khojasteh, Hamed Nemati, Michael Backes
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31119v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Resource disaggregation separates memory and accelerators from compute nodes and makes them remotely accessible. This improves resource sharing, but also removes the local kernel from the resource-access path. Under an untrusted host, compromised host software may use stale authority, exceed delegated authority, or reuse authority provisioned for another process. Prior work identifies capability-based access control as well suited to these architectures. Our systematization of twenty-two prior capability systems finds that none combines host-independent validation of process authority, authoritative enforcement at the resource, and revocation that remains effective while remote authorization state is stale. We present SADRA, a distributed capability-based access-control system for resource-disaggregated architectures. SmartNIC hardware isolated from host software independently checks every inter-node request at two points, first at the compute node against the requesting process's authority and again at the resource against the current authoritative access state. Linked process, compute, and resource capabilities allow these checks to use local state without coordination on the access path. When distributed authority is revoked, SADRA denies subsequent dependent accesses at the resource without waiting for remote nodes to update, while stale capability state is reclaimed separately. We prove capability safety, authority safety, revocation soundness, and strong isolation for a formal architectural model, and model-check the formalization with SPIN. Our FPGA SmartNIC prototype sustains 89.5 Gbit/s aggregate throughput, within run-to-run variation of a non-enforcing baseline that peaks at 90--91 Gbit/s. Cleanup of a 128-capability subtree completes in 528 ns, while access denial does not depend on completion of that cleanup.
tldr: SADRA is a distributed capability-based access-control system for resource-disaggregated architectures that enforces authority checks at both compute and resource nodes via an isolated SmartNIC, with formally verified safety and revocation properties.
motivation: Resource disaggregation removes the local kernel from the resource-access path, so under an untrusted host, compromised software can use stale, excessive, or reused authority; existing capability systems fail to combine host-independent validation, authoritative enforcement at the resource, and revocation effective under stale remote state.
method: The authors systematize twenty-two prior capability systems, then design SADRA using linked process, compute, and resource capabilities checked at two points by host-isolated SmartNIC hardware, proving capability safety, authority safety, revocation soundness, and strong isolation for a formal model model-checked with SPIN.
result: An FPGA SmartNIC prototype sustains 89.5 Gbit/s aggregate throughput, within run-to-run variation of a 90-91 Gbit/s non-enforcing baseline, and cleans up a 128-capability subtree in 528 ns while access denial remains independent of cleanup completion.
conclusion: SADRA demonstrates that hardware-enforced, host-independent distributed capability access control can deliver sound revocation and strong isolation in disaggregated architectures with negligible performance overhead.

title: Resource-Optimized And Energy-Aware Agentic Ai Framework Anchored On Blockchain For Secure Software Supply Chains
authors: Asadullah Abdullah Khan Toqeer Ali Syed
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31282v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a blockchain-backed agentic security framework designed to safeguard the complete software development lifecycle (SDLC) while also securing the agentic AI components responsible for monitoring it. The framework coordinates a set of specialised security agents, covering source integrity, dependency and SBOM analysis, CI configura tion auditing, artifact verification, and runtime policy evaluation, each supported by a large language model (LLM) that interprets artefacts, reasons over tool outputs, and produces structured security reports. To ensure agent trustworthiness, every agent generates a cryptographically signed attestation that is recorded in a permissioned blockchain via smart contracts, including an agent registry, an immutable attestation log, and an enforceable release-policy module. Communication among agents and with blockchain nodes is secured using a consortium-operated certificate authority, ensuring authenticated and tamper-resistant interactions. A detailed use-case and sequence flow demonstrate how a source code security agent performs analysis, anchors its attestation on-chain, and triggers a verifiable allow/block deployment decision. The proposed framework of fers decentralised integrity transparent provenance, uninterrupted security assurance and a generalisable architecture to incorporate the agentic AI into the modern software supply chain security.
tldr: The paper proposes a blockchain-backed agentic AI framework using LLM-driven security agents with signed on-chain attestations to secure the software supply chain and SDLC.
motivation: Modern software supply chains and the agentic AI systems that monitor them lack trustworthy provenance, tamper-resistance, and verifiable decision-making, motivating a decentralized security architecture.
method: Specialized LLM-based security agents (source integrity, dependency/SBOM analysis, CI auditing, artifact verification, runtime policy) generate cryptographically signed attestations recorded via smart contracts on a permissioned blockchain, with a consortium-operated CA securing communications.
result: A detailed use-case and sequence flow demonstrate a source code security agent performing analysis, anchoring its attestation on-chain, and triggering a verifiable allow/block deployment decision.
conclusion: The framework offers decentralized integrity, transparent provenance, uninterrupted security assurance, and a generalizable architecture for integrating agentic AI into software supply chain security.

title: AgentXploit: Autonomous Repository-to-Runtime Red-Teaming For Ai Agents
authors: Weida Liang, Shi Qiu, Zhun Wang, Simon Sure, Xiaoyuan Liu, Tianneng Shi, Zhaorun Chen, Wenbo Guo, Dawn Song
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31318v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents combine language models with external data and tools that can modify files, call APIs, or execute code. Security failures can arise when adversarial content changes an agent's tool use or when the surrounding software contains vulnerabilities such as path traversal or command injection. We study authorized white-box pre-deployment auditing, where the auditor has access to the target repository and a controlled runtime, but successful attacks must still act through the task-defined attacker interface and be confirmed by an external verifier. We present AgentXploit, a two-role auditing system that separates repository-level attack-path discovery from runtime exploitation. The Analyzer Agent traces attacker-controlled inputs to sensitive operations and records code-supported candidate attack paths; the Exploiter Agent turns these paths into concrete attacks and revises them using runtime feedback. We also introduce AgentXploit-Bench, containing 72 reproducible vulnerabilities across 12 open-source AI-agent systems and frameworks. Across three runs, AgentXploit reaches 59.3% end-to-end success, compared with 38.4% for Codex. Under a token-budget-matched comparison, Codex reaches 46.3%. On AgentDojo, where injection points are provided, the Exploiter Agent reaches 79.2% attack success versus 52.7% for AgentVigil. These results highlight repository discovery and runtime exploitation as distinct challenges in end-to-end agent security auditing.
tldr: AgentXploit is a two-role autonomous red-teaming system that separates repository-level attack-path discovery from runtime exploitation to audit AI agents for security vulnerabilities.
motivation: AI agents that call tools, modify files, and execute code can be compromised by adversarial content or software flaws such as path traversal and command injection, motivating authorized white-box pre-deployment auditing.
method: The Analyzer Agent traces attacker-controlled inputs to sensitive operations and records code-supported candidate attack paths, while the Exploiter Agent converts these into concrete attacks refined by runtime feedback; a new 72-vulnerability benchmark across 12 agent systems is introduced.
result: AgentXploit achieves 59.3% end-to-end attack success versus 38.4% for Codex (46.3% under matched token budget), and on AgentDojo the Exploiter reaches 79.2% attack success versus 52.7% for AgentVigil, with no quantum component.
conclusion: The work frames repository discovery and runtime exploitation as distinct challenges in end-to-end AI agent security auditing.

title: The Importance Of The Change-of-variables Integration Technique In Deriving The PDFs Of Important Probability Distributions
authors: Jorge P. Arpasi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30529v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The purpose of this article is to explicitly describe how the integration technique known as the change of variables is used in graduate-level Probability and Statistics courses. Throughout the article, we employ this integration technique seven times across various examples and results. We demonstrate that four applications of this technique are required to derive the probability density function (PDF) of the Student's t-distribution.
tldr: A pedagogical article demonstrating repeated use of the change-of-variables integration technique to derive probability density functions of standard distributions, including the Student's t-distribution.
motivation: Graduate-level probability and statistics students often struggle with the technical integration steps needed to derive PDFs of important distributions, and the change-of-variables technique is central to this task.
method: The author applies the change-of-variables integration technique seven times across worked examples and derivations, with four of those applications dedicated to obtaining the PDF of the Student's t-distribution.
result: A step-by-step exposition showing explicitly how the change-of-variables method yields the PDFs of several standard probability distributions.
conclusion: The article serves as an instructional resource emphasizing the importance and versatility of the change-of-variables technique in graduate statistics curricula.

title: Binary Dimension-free Discretization And Polynomial Complexification On Real Cubes
authors: Luis Miguel Casta\~no-Mar\'in, Daniel N\'u\~nez-Alarc\'on, Joedson Santos
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30587v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be the optimal dimension-free ratio between the polytorus and Boolean-cube norms of complex multiaffine polynomials of degree at most [MATH]. For every [MATH], [MATH] equals the unrestricted complexification constant of the real cube for complex polynomials of degree at most [MATH]. Moreover, [MATH], and for every [MATH], [MATH], where [MATH].
tldr: The paper studies optimal dimension-free ratios between polytorus and Boolean-cube norms for complex multiaffine polynomials and relates them to the complexification constant of real cubes.
motivation: It aims to resolve extremal norm inequalities and complexification constants for high-dimensional polynomials on real cubes, a pure mathematical problem in Banach space and polynomial analysis.
method: The authors analyze multiaffine polynomials and compare their norms on the polytorus and Boolean cube, deriving dimension-free constants via extremal and complexification arguments.
result: They show that the optimal ratio equals the unrestricted complexification constant for complex polynomials of each degree, and provide explicit bounds for all degrees.
conclusion: The work advances the mathematical theory of polynomial norm discretization and complexification, but it does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Concurrent Parameter Learning And Current Control For Large-scale Grid-following Inverter-based Resources
authors: Satish Vedula
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30723v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The integration of large-scale inverter-based resources (IBRs) into the grid presents two key challenges in terms of optimal power generation and transmission system stability. This work proposes concurrent transmission parameter learning and optimal power generation and current control for the grid-following IBRs. The proposed approach estimates transmission parameters online using the current measurements, enabling the IBRs to adapt their control actions to evolving grid conditions. The learned parameter estimates are incorporated into an optimization-based power distribution strategy to determine the optimal power setpoints. In parallel, a current control scheme is designed to regulate the grid-following (GFL) IBRs current output based on the estimates and received active and reactive power references from the high-level optimizer, thereby improving the dynamic response to the grid events. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is validated through a simulation in a MATLAB-Simulink environment. From the results, the impact of the concurrent estimator and current controller during the grid events can be seen.
tldr: This paper proposes a framework that concurrently learns transmission-line parameters online and performs optimal power-setpoint and current control for large-scale grid-following inverter-based resources.
motivation: Integrating large-scale inverter-based resources into power grids creates challenges for optimal power generation and transmission system stability, particularly when grid conditions evolve and parameters are unknown.
method: Transmission parameters are estimated online from current measurements, and the estimates are fed into an optimization-based power distribution strategy that computes setpoints, while a current controller regulates the GFL inverter output using those estimates and the active/reactive power references from the high-level optimizer.
result: MATLAB-Simulink simulations show the combined estimator and current controller improving dynamic response during grid events, with the impact of concurrent estimation and control being visible in the results.
conclusion: The proposed concurrent parameter-learning and current-control scheme appears effective for grid-following IBRs, though validation is limited to simulation.

title: Hyponormal Toeplitz Operators With Operator Valued Normal Symbols
authors: Pratima Pandey Neeru Bala
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30801v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article, we first give a characterization of hyponormal Toeplitz operators with operator valued normal symbols. Latter, we examine when the class of hyponormal Toeplitz operators with operator valued symbols are analytic or normal.
tldr: The paper characterizes hyponormal Toeplitz operators with operator-valued normal symbols and studies when such operators are analytic or normal.
motivation: Toeplitz operators with operator-valued symbols are a classical object in operator theory and functional analysis, and hyponormality conditions remain incompletely understood in this setting.
method: Pure operator-theoretic analysis on Hardy/Bergman-type spaces, deriving algebraic conditions on operator-valued normal symbols that guarantee hyponormality, analyticity, or normality.
result: A characterization of hyponormal Toeplitz operators with operator-valued normal symbols is given, together with criteria under which such operators are analytic or normal.
conclusion: The results extend classical Toeplitz operator theory to the operator-valued symbol case, but they have no evident connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Dynamic Service Recommendation With Congestion-Dependent Joining: Near-Optimal And Constant-Factor Approximation Algorithms
authors: Yi-Chun Akchen, Sena Asli Bozkurt, Chen-An Lin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30812v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern service platforms often provide customers with real-time congestion information, such as anticipated waiting times, before they decide whether to use a service. This creates an intertemporal tradeoff in service recommendation: directing a customer to a service may generate immediate value, but the resulting congestion can make that service less attractive to future customers. We study this tradeoff through a finite-horizon stochastic optimization problem in which a platform dynamically recommends among multiple services, each represented by a queue, with customers' joining probabilities decreasing with congestion. We first formulate the problem as a Markov decision process and show that optimal decisions generally depend on the joint congestion state, giving rise to a prohibitively large state space. We develop two complementary approximation algorithms that overcome this curse of dimensionality. First, we provide a quasi-polynomial-time approximation scheme that uses truncation and rounding of the model primitives to compress the joint congestion state, while carefully accounting for how these approximations affect the stochastic evolution of the system to establish near-optimality. Second, we develop a polynomial-time LP-guided algorithm that replaces the joint-state representation with service-level marginal information and achieves a (1-1/e) approximation guarantee under substantially more general service and joining dynamics. Finally, we show that monotone joining behavior, whereby customers become less likely to join as a service becomes more congested, marks a fundamental tractability boundary: without monotonicity, the problem is NP-hard to approximate within any constant factor. This establishes monotonicity as a key behavioral property that enables tractable dynamic service recommendation despite the complexity introduced by congestion-dependent joining.
tldr: The paper studies dynamic service recommendation when customers' joining probabilities decrease with congestion, using stochastic optimization and approximation algorithms.
motivation: Real-time congestion information creates an intertemporal tradeoff: recommending a service may yield immediate value but can worsen future congestion and reduce future demand.
method: The problem is formulated as a finite-horizon Markov decision process with a prohibitively large joint congestion state; two approximation algorithms are developed: a quasi-polynomial-time approximation scheme based on truncation and rounding, and a polynomial-time LP-guided algorithm using service-level marginal information.
result: The LP-guided algorithm achieves a (1-1/e) approximation guarantee under monotone joining behavior, and without monotonicity the problem is NP-hard to approximate within any constant factor.
conclusion: Monotone joining behavior is identified as a fundamental tractability boundary that enables efficient dynamic service recommendation despite congestion-dependent complexity.

title: Can Pixels Alone Reveal Image Origin? Minimax Limits And Learnable Interfaces For Passive Provenance
authors: Kai Yao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Passive image provenance asks whether pixels alone can reveal where an image came from: a human, an aggregate AI class, or a particular generator. This becomes a robustness problem once a source image can be edited before the verifier sees it. We study the problem as source--target verification under adversarial distribution shift. Our first result gives the exact best-case limit for any image-only verifier: the largest robust target-acceptance gap equals the minimum total-variation distance between the target distribution and the set of attacked source distributions. This quantity depends on the source, target, and edit class, not on the verifier architecture. Our second result explains why deployed public verifiers can fail before this statistical limit is reached. If the verifier can be emulated on the attack region to error [MATH], then a surrogate black-box attack reaches target acceptance within [MATH] plus optimization error of the white-box optimum; score-revealing logistic and softmax heads over public features are identifiable, and approximate score access gives stable recovery bounds. A finite-state experiment checks the minimax identity where both sides are computable. On same-prompt real/diffusion benchmarks, the evaluated public CLIP verifiers fail under targeted pixel attacks, while a ResNet-18 victim exhibits partial fake-to-real transfer. Binary feedback with abstention reduces measured attack success, but positive empirical gap upper bounds do not establish robustness. These results motivate separate evaluation of the source--target statistical ceiling and the information released by a deployed verifier.
tldr: The paper studies passive image provenance under adversarial distribution shift, deriving minimax limits for image-only verifiers and showing that deployed CLIP verifiers can fail under targeted pixel attacks.
motivation: It asks whether pixels alone can reliably reveal image origin, especially when a source image may be edited before verification, framing provenance as source-target verification under adversarial distribution shift.
method: The authors derive an exact best-case limit via minimum total-variation distance between the target distribution and attacked source distributions, and analyze surrogate black-box attacks against score-revealing verifier heads.
result: The robust target-acceptance gap equals the stated TV-distance limit, public CLIP verifiers fail under targeted pixel attacks while a ResNet-18 victim shows partial fake-to-real transfer, and binary feedback with abstention reduces measured attack success.
conclusion: The work motivates separately evaluating the source-target statistical ceiling and the information released by a deployed verifier, rather than treating positive empirical gap upper bounds as proof of robustness.

title: Breaking The Black Box: Byte-Level Boundary Inference Of Real-World Antivirus Systems
authors: Jieshuai Yang, Zhi Wang, Yan Jia, Zhenhua Wu, Jianfei Tang, Chenbin Su, Jingwei Ye, Jianwen Tian, Wanpeng Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing approaches for understanding the detection logic of real-world antivirus (AV) software infer only binary malware/benign decisions from black-box queries, providing limited insight into the fine-grained decision-critical regions that govern AV detection. In this paper, we present , the first framework for inferring byte-level decision-critical regions of real-world AV products under a black-box threat model. AVHunter constructs the first large-scale Byte-Level AV Boundary Dataset (BABD) by systematically probing 11 real-world AV products, revealing that modern AV detections are largely associated with a small number of compact decision-critical byte regions. Leveraging BABD, AVHunter trains AV-specific models that not only reproduce binary AV decisions, but also localize the decision-critical byte regions underlying these decisions, achieving an average boundary prediction recall of 85.07% while maintaining 97.43% detection agreement with the target AVs. We further validate that the predicted regions capture genuine AV decision knowledge through boundary-guided malware evasion, false-positive induction on benign executables, and a seven-month longitudinal study demonstrating that the inferred regions remain largely stable as AV products evolve. Overall, AVHunter moves beyond conventional binary-label AV modeling by enabling fine-grained boundary-region localization and revealing a new form of AV knowledge leakage with important implications for malware analysis, AV security, and boundary-aware defenses.
tldr: AVHunter is a black-box framework that infers byte-level decision-critical regions of real-world antivirus engines, enabling fine-grained localization beyond binary malware/benign labels.
motivation: Existing black-box AV analysis only recovers binary decisions, giving little insight into the compact byte regions that actually drive detection. The authors aim to expose and characterize those decision-critical boundaries.
method: The framework systematically probes 11 real-world AV products to build the Byte-Level AV Boundary Dataset (BABD), then trains AV-specific models that jointly reproduce binary decisions and localize the responsible byte regions.
result: The models achieve 85.07% average boundary prediction recall and 97.43% detection agreement, and the inferred regions are validated via boundary-guided evasion, false-positive induction on benign files, and a seven-month longitudinal stability study.
conclusion: The work reveals a new form of AV knowledge leakage and argues for boundary-aware defenses, though the findings are confined to malware/AV security and have no connection to quantum information science.

title: Machine Unlearning For Large Language Models: Foundations, Advances, And Agentic Extensions
authors: Xiaoyu Xu, Minxin Du, Li Bai, Junxu Liu, Yaxin Xiao, Kun Fang, Liu Yang, Huadi Zheng, Peizhao Hu, Qingqing Ye, Haibo Hu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30909v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine unlearning aims to remove target influence while preserving other capabilities. This survey compares methods, benchmarks, and evidence across large language models and systems using retrieval, memory, tools, and interacting agents. A five-layer framework connects removal requests, system boundaries, target locations, interventions, and supported claims. A seven-stage lifecycle and six evidence dimensions guide comparison. The review shows that target construction, retained data, and recovery tests affect reported outcomes. Evidence from model evaluations remains insufficient to establish removal across external state and subsequent updates, motivating evaluation that tracks dependencies and tests whether target influence returns.
tldr: This survey reviews machine unlearning methods, benchmarks, and evidence for large language models and agentic systems.
motivation: Machine unlearning aims to remove target influence from models while preserving other capabilities, but evaluation and scope for LLM systems remain unclear.
method: It proposes a five-layer framework, a seven-stage lifecycle, and six evidence dimensions to compare unlearning approaches and their claimed removal guarantees.
result: It finds that target construction, retained data, and recovery tests strongly affect reported outcomes, and current model evaluations are insufficient for removal across external state and subsequent updates.
conclusion: The review motivates dependency-tracking evaluation and recovery tests to verify whether target influence truly disappears.

title: Prompt Injection Detection For Email Agents Through Attack Chain Modeling
authors: Ahmad Hashmi, Dhyey Patel, Yunting Yin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30657v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model email assistants are particularly vulnerable to indirect prompt injection because untrusted email content can be retrieved into the model context and influence subsequent tool use. Existing prompt injection detectors mainly formulate this problem as binary malicious text classification, which overlooks the important factor that harmful agent behavior often arises through a sequence of stages. We propose a detection framework that models this attack chain by combining a text detector, verifiers specific to each stage, explicit rule-based risk signals, user intent and action consistency analysis, and a logistic decision policy. To support this framework, we derive attack chain labels from prompt injection datasets, evaluate the proposed framework under random splits, temporal phase transfer, conditional stage transfer, cross-dataset transfer, and conduct ablation studies on multiple benchmarks. Results show that random train test splits substantially overestimate robustness under distribution shift, while later tool argument stages are more predictable than earlier stages in the framework. We also show that training on harmless emails that resemble attacks helps reduce false alarms while preserving the ability to detect real attacks. Across five binary benchmarks, our framework achieves a mean F1 score of 0.406 under the strict threshold setting policy, compared with 0.216 for the strongest of five pretrained detectors evaluated without additional training. These results highlight the value of combining attack stage predictions with checks for conflicts between the user's request and instructions in retrieved emails. Our experiments also demonstrate the importance of training with challenging benign examples to balance attack detection and false alarms.
tldr: The paper proposes a prompt injection detection framework for LLM email agents by modeling attack chains with text detectors, stage verifiers, rule-based signals, and user intent consistency analysis.
motivation: Large language model email assistants are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection because untrusted email content can enter the model context and influence tool use, while existing detectors treat this as binary malicious text classification and miss staged attack progression.
method: The authors derive attack chain labels from prompt injection datasets and combine a text detector, stage-specific verifiers, explicit rule-based risk signals, user intent/action consistency analysis, and a logistic decision policy, evaluating under random splits, temporal phase transfer, conditional stage transfer, cross-dataset transfer, and ablations.
result: Random train-test splits substantially overestimate robustness under distribution shift; later tool argument stages are more predictable than earlier stages; training on harmless attack-like emails reduces false alarms while preserving detection. Across five binary benchmarks, the framework achieves mean F1 0.406 under a strict threshold policy versus 0.216 for the strongest of five pretrained detectors without additional training.
conclusion: Combining attack stage predictions with checks for conflicts between user requests and instructions in retrieved emails improves detection, and training with challenging benign examples helps balance attack detection and false alarms.

title: Agate: Provenance-Based Runtime Defense Against Compositional Attacks On Llm Agents
authors: Xiaorui Zhang, Zhuoran Cheng, Kailin Liu, Zhaoxi Sun, Shiyu Fan, Tongyu Yuan, Bin Yuan, Weizhong Qiang, Deqing Zou
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30830v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents can produce harmful effects through sequences of ordinary operations. Judging such actions requires establishing both the authority that permits them and the origin of the data they carry. We present AGATE, an authorization and data-provenance gate at instrumented agent-harness boundaries. Operator declarations and host approval events ground authorization; delegated actions are constrained by grants that bind to exact parameters, expire, and permit a limited number of uses. Source registration connects observed inputs to subsequent transfers, while an effect ledger tracks repeated requests. Deterministic checks make decisions without an LLM in the decision path and retain their grounds with execution evidence for forensic replay. Adapters integrate three production harnesses -- DeepSeek Harness, OpenCode, and OpenClaw -- without modifying host code, translating each host's native observation and veto points into a single shared gate interface; the judgment core is identical in all three, and only enforcement depth differs. Our evaluation combines 153 exercised attack-chain records with deployment, utility, and reconstruction experiments. The deployment observations expose how tool declarations and data checks govern business actions, including a bypass through parameter rewriting. Six of eleven benign file-processing scenarios contain denial events, revealing the utility cost of content-based provenance policies. Across 252 runs on 63 sanitized scenarios, replay agrees with live graph projections for all 63 scenarios on each of two platforms. These results establish the feasibility of provenance-based runtime judgment and identify content transformation, legitimate reuse, and observation coverage as concrete limits.
tldr: AGATE is a provenance-based runtime authorization and data-provenance gate that defends LLM agents against compositional attacks.
motivation: LLM agents can produce harmful effects through sequences of ordinary operations, so runtime judgment must establish both the authority permitting actions and the origin of data they carry.
method: AGATE uses operator declarations, host approval events, parameter-bound grants, source registration, and an effect ledger, with deterministic checks and adapters for three production harnesses.
result: Evaluation over 153 attack-chain records and 252 runs on 63 sanitized scenarios shows replay agreement with live graph projections, while benign file-processing scenarios reveal utility costs and policy limits.
conclusion: The results establish the feasibility of provenance-based runtime judgment for LLM agents and identify content transformation, legitimate reuse, and observation coverage as concrete limitations.

title: Symmetric Kahane--Salem--Zygmund Inequalities And The Supremum Norm
authors: Daniel M. Pellegrino, Anselmo B. Raposo Jr., Eduardo V. Teixeira
abstract: ArXiv:2609.30663v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Kahane--Salem--Zygmund inequality provides unimodular [MATH]-linear forms with small supremum norm. We consider its dimension-free symmetric constant [MATH] over the real scalar field, defined by the requirement that, for every [MATH], some real symmetric unimodular [MATH]-linear form [MATH] satisfy \[ \|A\|\le C_m^{}n^{(m+1)/2}. \] For complex scalars, Boas obtained under permutation symmetry an upper bound of order at most [MATH]; over the real scalar field, an elementary argument gives the sharper order [MATH]. We prove \[ C_m^{}\ge \left(+o(1)\right)}m, \] using the square-free Walsh spectrum of the diagonal polynomial. In the opposite direction, we establish \[ C_m^{}\le C_0, \] where [MATH] is absolute, removing the factor [MATH] from the real upper bound. This estimate follows from a geometric argument in which rigidity for Gram permanents reduces the relevant configurations to sets controlled by Gaussian width. For unrestricted unimodular forms, we also obtain a quantitative rectangular estimate from truncated Hadamard matrices; in equal dimension, the normalized minimum is at most [MATH] whenever [MATH].
tldr: The paper studies the symmetric constant in the Kahane-Salem-Zygmund inequality for unimodular multilinear forms over real scalars, proving new lower and upper bounds.
motivation: The Kahane-Salem-Zygmund inequality provides unimodular m-linear forms with small supremum norm, and the dimension-free symmetric constant C_m is central to understanding the optimal order of this norm.
method: The authors use the square-free Walsh spectrum of the diagonal polynomial to prove a lower bound and a geometric argument involving rigidity for Gram permanents and Gaussian width to establish an upper bound.
result: They show C_m >= (1+o(1))^m and C_m <= C_0, where C_0 is an absolute constant, removing the factor from the real upper bound, and also obtain a quantitative rectangular estimate from truncated Hadamard matrices.
conclusion: The work significantly tightens the known bounds for the symmetric constant, resolving the order in the real case and providing new tools from harmonic analysis and geometric functional analysis.
